puzzles.funFact: The Mekong River carries so much sediment that the delta around Can Tho is actually growing — it extends further into the sea by about 30 metres every year. But rising sea levels and upstream dams are now reversing this, and parts of the delta are sinking for the first time in recorded history.

photo.description: a group of people on a boat in the water

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A lakeside village so picturesque it inspired a replica in China — and has been inhabited for 7,000 years.
clues: This village clings to a narrow strip of land between a steep mountain and a deep lake — so constrained that for centuries, the only access was by boat.
Its salt mine, still operating today, is the oldest in the world — salt extracted here funded the Iron Age culture that archaeologists named after this very place.

In 2011, a Chinese company secretly photographed every corner of the village and built an exact replica in Guangdong Province — the villagers discovered this when tourists started arriving with printouts of the Chinese version.
Its church charnel house contains over 1,200 decorated skulls — when the graveyard ran out of space, bones were exhumed, bleached, painted with flowers and names, and displayed on shelves.
Located in Austria, this village of fewer than 800 permanent residents was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997 and now draws over a million visitors annually.
puzzles.funFact: The Hallstatt salt mine is so old that archaeologists have found perfectly preserved wooden tools, leather shoes, and even a Bronze Age backpack inside — kept intact for thousands of years by the antiseptic properties of the salt.

photo.description: houses near body of water and mountain during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A shallow, blood-red soda lake edged with white salt crusts on the floor of the East African Rift, with a flock of pink flamingos wading in the shallows and a volcanic cone rising hazily in the distance.
clues: Deep in East Africa's Rift Valley, a shallow lake glows in shades of red and orange, its water so alkaline it can burn the skin and eyes of animals not adapted to it.

Surface temperatures here can top 40°C, yet this hostile water is the main breeding ground in East Africa for lesser flamingos, whose nests of mud sit on salt-crusted flats that keep most land predators away.
Birds and bats that die along its shores can be left crusted in soda and salt, preserved like statues, a haunting sight made famous by photographer Nick Brandt's images.
Just to the south, a cone the Maasai call the 'Mountain of God' is the only volcano known to have erupted carbonatite lava, which flows black and then bleaches pale as it weathers.

Lying in northern Tanzania close to the Kenyan border, it is fed by a river rising in Kenya and by mineral-rich hot springs; with no outlet, its water escapes only by evaporation, leaving crusts of soda behind.
puzzles.funFact: The lake is named after natron, the natural mix of sodium carbonate and baking soda that ancient Egyptians used to dry out mummies. Here, evaporation leaves the same kind of salts in thick crusts along its shores.
puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A blood-red lake in East Africa so caustic that almost nothing lives there, except flamingos.

photo.description: flock of flamingos on water during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Karst peaks rising from a flat river valley — the landscape on the back of China's 20-yuan note.
clues: The landscape here formed over 300 million years as limestone dissolved and eroded into hundreds of sharp, forested peaks rising abruptly from flat farmland and river plains.
Cormorant fishermen still work this river using trained birds on leashes — a practice over a thousand years old, though today it is largely performed for tourists.
The scene is so iconic in its country that it was chosen to represent the nation on its 20-yuan banknote.
Located in the Guangxi region of southern China, the river cruise between its two main towns is considered one of the most scenic river journeys in Asia.

When US President Bill Clinton cruised these waters in 1998, he marvelled that the scenery made him think of a traditional Chinese painting — and no wonder: this stretch of southern China, its glassy green river curling past jade limestone peaks, is the picture-postcard image the world pictures when it imagines the Chinese landscape.
puzzles.funFact: The Li River's karst landscape inspired the floating mountains of Pandora in James Cameron's Avatar — Cameron's team visited the region specifically to photograph the peaks as reference material for the film's alien geology.

photo.description: people riding on boat on lake during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A UNESCO town at the confluence of two rivers — where monks in saffron collect alms at dawn and French colonial buildings line the streets.
clues: Every morning before sunrise, hundreds of Buddhist monks walk silently through the streets collecting food offerings from local residents — a ceremony that has continued unbroken for centuries.

The streets here feel like two worlds collided and never separated — gilded temple rooftops rise above French colonial shophouses, and saffron-robed monks pass whitewashed facades with shuttered windows.
Temple compounds outnumber city blocks here — this town has more than thirty active wats within walking distance of each other, each with resident monks who maintain them daily.

Located in a landlocked country in Southeast Asia, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage City in 1995 — one of the first in the region — in recognition of its remarkably intact traditional architecture.

A short drive away, the Kuang Si waterfall cascades through turquoise travertine pools bright enough to look artificial — and at the forest above it, a sanctuary rescues sun bears confiscated from the illegal wildlife trade.
puzzles.funFact: The tak bat alms ceremony has become so popular with tourists that UNESCO has issued warnings about its commercialization — some monks have stopped participating because tourists photograph them with flash cameras at close range during the silent predawn ritual.

photo.description: Buddhist monks receive alms in the early morning

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The end of the world — an archipelago of glaciers, peat bogs, and penguin colonies where the wind never stops.
clues: This place sits at the southern tip of the Americas — so remote that the city here bills itself as the southernmost in the world, and ships heading to Antarctica pass through its waters.
It was named by Ferdinand Magellan in 1520 when he saw fires lit by the indigenous people along the shoreline as his fleet passed through the strait that now bears his name.
Darwin visited during his voyage on the Beagle and was so struck by the indigenous people here that his observations shaped his thinking about human adaptation to extreme environments.
It is split between two countries — Argentina to the east and Chile to the west — divided by a straight line that makes it one of the most unusual borders on Earth.

Located at the southern tip of South America, its main Argentine city — Ushuaia, which bills itself as the southernmost city in the world — sits on the shores of a wide bay surrounded by mountains and is the gateway for most Antarctic expedition cruises.
puzzles.funFact: The Yaghan people who lived here for thousands of years wore almost no clothing despite temperatures near freezing — they coated themselves in animal fat and kept fires burning constantly, including in their canoes. Darwin was astonished; the Yaghan found his clothing absurd.

photo.description: a body of water with mountains in the back

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Pale limestone towers turning pink at sunset — the Alps' most dramatic skyline.
clues: These mountains glow pink and orange at sunset and sunrise — a phenomenon caused by the pale rock catching low-angle light, and it has a name in the local dialect that translates roughly as 'turning rosy.'
They formed from ancient coral reefs — what are now peaks over 3,000 metres high were once flat seabed, and fossil seashells are still found near the summits.

During World War I, the front line ran through these mountains — soldiers on both sides tunnelled into the glaciers and detonated explosives inside the rock, and bodies are still being recovered from melting ice today.
Located in northeastern Italy near the Austrian border, they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Europe's premier ski destinations in winter.
The Three Peaks — three vertical towers of pale rock rising from a high plateau — are their most iconic formation, appearing on postcards and climbing magazines worldwide.
puzzles.funFact: The mineral dolomite — which gives these mountains their name and colour — was identified here by French geologist Déodat Gratet de Dolomieu in 1788. He noticed the rock didn't fizz when acid was applied, unlike normal limestone, and realized it was a previously unknown mineral.

photo.description: Purple flowers bloom before majestic mountains

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A nation of coral rings in the Indian Ocean — the lowest country on Earth, threatened by the sea that surrounds it.
clues: This nation consists of 26 atolls and over 1,000 coral islands — but its average elevation above sea level is less than one metre, making it the lowest-lying country on Earth.
Scientists predict that without intervention, most of its islands could be uninhabitable by 2100 due to rising sea levels — making it the most climate-vulnerable nation on the planet.
It was the first country in the world to hold a cabinet meeting underwater — in 2009, the president and ministers donned scuba gear to sign a document calling for global carbon emission reductions.
Located in the Indian Ocean southwest of Sri Lanka, it is the smallest country in Asia by land area but one of the most spread-out — its islands stretch across 900 kilometres of ocean.

Its luxury overwater resorts have made it synonymous with honeymoon travel — though the government is quietly purchasing land in neighbouring countries as a potential relocation site for its entire population.
puzzles.funFact: The Maldives has a contingency plan: the government has been purchasing land in Australia, India, and Sri Lanka as a potential relocation site for its entire population if the islands become uninhabitable. The country is preparing for its own disappearance.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A city of vintage cars, crumbling baroque facades, and music spilling from every doorway.
clues: The streets here are filled with American cars from the 1950s — kept running through improvisation and ingenuity for decades after a trade embargo made new parts impossible to obtain.
Its old city centre is one of the best-preserved colonial urban areas in the Americas, with Spanish baroque buildings dating to the 16th century.
The city was founded by the Spanish in 1519 and grew wealthy as the staging point for treasure fleets carrying gold and silver from the Americas back to Europe.
Its seafront promenade is famous as a gathering place where locals sit at dusk watching the sun drop into the water — and the sea spray regularly soaks anyone sitting too close to the wall.
A famous American author lived here for nearly 20 years and his favourite bar still serves the drink he reportedly consumed daily — a bronze statue of him stands at the spot where he always stood.
puzzles.funFact: Cuba has more classic American cars per capita than any country in the world — including the United States. When the embargo began in 1962, there were about 150,000 American cars in Cuba. There are still roughly 60,000 operating today, maintained entirely without American spare parts.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: The world's largest intact volcanic caldera — a self-contained ecosystem where predator and prey live on the same stage.
clues: This is the largest intact volcanic caldera on Earth — a collapsed volcano whose walls form a natural enclosure about 20 kilometres across and 600 metres deep.
The crater walls are steep enough that most large animals do not leave — creating a self-sustaining ecosystem with one of the highest predator densities anywhere in Africa.
It contains one of the densest concentrations of wildlife on the continent: lions, elephants, rhinos, hippos, flamingos, and wildebeest all share a space smaller than some cities.
Located in northern Tanzania, it was formed by a massive volcanic collapse roughly 2 to 3 million years ago and is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It is one of the few places on Earth where you can see lion, elephant, buffalo, black rhinoceros, and hippopotamus — five of Africa's most iconic species — in a single day.
puzzles.funFact: The lions of Ngorongoro are genetically distinct from lions elsewhere in Africa — centuries of living within the crater walls has made them more inbred than any other lion population on Earth. Scientists monitor them closely because their limited gene pool makes them vulnerable to disease.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: Emerald steps carved into a hillside — an ancient irrigation system so sophisticated it shapes an entire culture.
clues: Curved terraces of vivid green descend a hillside in concentric rings, each level flooded so it mirrors the sky — and the entire system has been governed not by engineers or governments but by a hierarchy of water temples for over a thousand years.

This system is not just agricultural — it is governed by spiritual principles that coordinate sharing between farmers across an entire landscape, and has operated continuously for over a thousand years.
UNESCO inscribed this landscape as a World Heritage Site in 2012, recognising it as a living cultural tradition that has shaped both the land and the society simultaneously.
Located in the cultural heartland of an Indonesian island where traditional dance, painting, and temple ceremony have been practiced without interruption for centuries.

In Eat, Pray, Love, Julia Roberts pedals a bicycle through these glowing green steps during her soul-searching stay on a famous Indonesian island — and travellers still come to ride the same lush paddies she did.
puzzles.funFact: The subak irrigation system is so effective at pest control that when the World Bank convinced Balinese farmers to abandon it in the 1970s in favour of modern farming methods, pest populations exploded. Within a decade, the traditional system was restored — and pest outbreaks stopped.

photo.description: a lush green rice field surrounded by palm trees

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest: A walled city on the Caribbean — where Spanish gold once left for Europe and bougainvillea spills over every colonial balcony.
clues: This city is enclosed by a massive colonial wall — built over decades by the Spanish to protect the most important port in the Americas, through which nearly all the gold and silver looted from the continent passed.
Its historic centre is a maze of narrow cobblestone streets where brightly coloured buildings with flower-draped balconies have remained largely unchanged since the 16th century.
It was attacked repeatedly by pirates and privateers — Francis Drake sacked it in 1586, and the Spanish responded by building fortifications that took over 200 years to complete.
Located on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, its old city and fortifications were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984 and are considered the best-preserved colonial port in the Americas.
Gabriel García Márquez set several of his novels here and lived in the city until his death, calling it the most beautiful city in the world.
puzzles.funFact: The walls of Cartagena took so long to build — over 200 years — that by the time they were finished, the era of pirate attacks was essentially over. Spain spent enormous treasure protecting treasure that had largely already been spent.

photo.description: Yellow historic clock tower in a sunny plaza

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city split by a gorge and bridged by centuries of ambition
clues: A city perched on the edge of a sheer cliff, cleaved in two by a dramatic gorge dropping nearly 100 metres to the river far below.
Its whitewashed buildings and iron balconies overlook rugged inland mountains shaped by centuries of Moorish and Christian contest.
During the Spanish Civil War, captured prisoners were thrown from the cliff into the gorge below — a scene Ernest Hemingway witnessed and documented in his writing.
Located in Andalusia, southern Spain, it gave birth to the modern tradition of bullfighting on foot, and its most iconic sight is the 300-year-old Puente Nuevo bridge.
Orson Welles was so enchanted by this cliffside Andalusian city that he requested his ashes be buried here — on a local bullfighter's estate, where they remain.
puzzles.funFact: Orson Welles visited Ronda obsessively throughout his life and asked to be buried there. His ashes now rest on a bullfighter's estate in the Andalusian hills — a man who made his name in Hollywood, permanently interred in a Spanish cliff-city.

photo.description: brown concrete building near green trees under blue sky during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a river that loses itself in the sands — and becomes something extraordinary
clues: A vast inland labyrinth of papyrus channels, lily-covered lagoons, and flooded islands that appears from above like a mosaic of blue and green.
The river feeding it flows not to the ocean but disappears into desert sand, creating a delta that blooms inland every year — a flood arriving paradoxically in the dry season.
Elephants, hippos, wild dogs, and lions all converge on this maze of waterways — one of the last places on Earth where the full suite of African megafauna gathers in one landscape.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site in southern Africa, it sits in a landlocked country home to over a third of the world's elephants.

Visitors glide silently through its flooded channels in slender dugout canoes, each pushed along by a standing poler with a long wooden pole — the southern-African answer to a Venetian gondola ride, and the most iconic way to drift past hippos and elephants here.
puzzles.funFact: The Okavango Delta is the only major river system on Earth that flows away from the ocean — it starts in Angola, travels over 1,000 km, and then simply disappears into the Kalahari sand without ever reaching the sea.

photo.description: aerial photography of body of water

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the oldest and deepest lake on Earth
clues: A vast crescent carved by ancient tectonic forces holds within its depths more liquid freshwater than any lake on Earth — its floor plunging so far down it sits below sea level.
In winter, its surface freezes into transparent blue ice metres thick — local tribes once drove across it by horse-drawn sled for months at a time.
It holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen surface freshwater and is home to a freshwater seal found nowhere else on Earth.
Situated in Siberia, Russia, this rift lake is geologically ancient — over 25 million years old — and surrounded by mountains and taiga forest.

When the world's longest railway met this frozen barrier on its run toward the Pacific, the icebreakers couldn't smash through the ice — so one desperate winter crews laid track straight across the frozen lake and had horses haul the wagons over, until a locomotive crashed through and sank into the deepest lake on Earth.
puzzles.funFact: Lake Baikal's nerpa seal evolved there independently from any ocean species — it is the only exclusively freshwater seal on Earth, and scientists still debate how its ancestors reached this landlocked Siberian lake millions of years ago.

photo.description: brown rock formation

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an ancient Nabataean city carved into rose-red cliffs — Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site
clues: More than 100 monumental tombs are carved directly into sandstone outcrops rising from a flat desert plain — their facades elaborately decorated despite the emptiness surrounding them.
The civilisation that built this place also built a more famous city to the north, connected by ancient trade routes carrying incense, spices, and silk across the Arabian peninsula.
For centuries it was sealed from the outside world — foreigners were forbidden entry, and the site sat largely unknown to travellers until it opened to tourism for the first time in 2020.
Located in the Al-Ula region of northwestern Saudi Arabia, it was the southern capital of the Nabataean kingdom, the same civilisation that built Petra in present-day Jordan.

When this long-sealed desert necropolis finally opened to the world, blind Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli sang the very first concert ever staged among its towering carved tombs — a world-first performance in the sands of Saudi Arabia that announced the kingdom's most spectacular ancient site was open at last.
puzzles.funFact: Hegra's tombs are more intact than Petra's because Saudi Arabia kept the site completely closed to outsiders for centuries — the isolation that made it unknown is precisely what preserved it so perfectly.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a fortress-palace that rises from its mountain like a continuation of the rock itself
clues: A thirteen-storey structure of whitewashed stone and red chapels climbs a rocky hill with a gravity that suggests it grew there rather than was built.
Its walls contain thousands of gilded statues, jewel-encrusted shrines, and sacred objects accumulated across centuries of continuous religious devotion.
Construction began in the 7th century and continued for decades — later rulers expanded it room by room, corridor by corridor, until it contained over 1,000 chambers.
For centuries the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas, it sits in Lhasa in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China.

Brad Pitt's 1997 film "Seven Years in Tibet" recreated this towering hilltop palace, where its young god-king was tutored by Pitt's real-life character — the same spiritual leader who fled over the Himalayas in 1959 and has lived in exile in India ever since, never permitted to return home.
puzzles.funFact: No complete inventory of the Potala Palace has ever been made — it contains over 1,000 rooms, and curators believe there are chambers that have not been entered in living memory.

photo.description: The potala palace towers above a mountain

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a monastery that clings to a cliff face like a dream refusing to fall
clues: A cluster of white and golden buildings clings impossibly to a vertical granite cliff, connected by a steep forested path winding through mountain mist.
The buildings are anchored directly into the rock face with no flat foundation — monks have lived and prayed here at altitude for over three centuries, sustained by supplies carried up by mule.
No one fully understands how it was built — the cliff face it occupies has no natural ledge, and the construction methods used in the 17th century remain a subject of scholarly debate.

High in the eastern Himalayas, it perches roughly 900 metres above the valley floor in a small, deeply Buddhist kingdom wedged between India and Tibet — a remote land of red-robed monks and fortress-monasteries that opened to outsiders only in recent decades.

Legend says an 8th-century guru flew to this sheer cliff on the back of a flying tigress, then meditated in a cave there to subdue a demon — the temple was later raised around that very grotto, and after a 1998 fire gutted it, devotees rebuilt it so faithfully that visitors can barely tell.
puzzles.funFact: The Tiger's Nest was largely destroyed by fire in 1998 and rebuilt so faithfully that most visitors cannot tell — the reconstruction used the same materials and traditional techniques as the 17th-century original, completed in just four years.

photo.description: a cliff with a building on top of it

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an Arctic archipelago where polar bears outnumber people
clues: A jagged archipelago of glaciers, tundra, and coal-black mountains sits at the edge of the navigable world, where the sky burns green or glows amber for months at a time.
Polar bears roam freely here — so freely that residents are required to carry rifles when venturing beyond the settlement limits.
Despite sitting at 78° north latitude, a warm ocean current keeps it navigable for much of the year, making it a base for polar expeditions since the 17th century.
An autonomous Norwegian territory, its main settlement Longyearbyen is one of the northernmost permanent communities on Earth.

For over half a century, no one new has been buried in its main settlement: the permafrost is so unrelenting that corpses never decompose — bodies from the 1918 flu pandemic were found eerily intact decades later — so today anyone gravely ill is flown to the mainland to die.
puzzles.funFact: It is technically illegal to die in Longyearbyen, Svalbard — because bodies do not decompose in the permafrost, residents who are gravely ill are flown to the mainland to die there instead.

photo.description: red and brown wooden houses on snow covered ground

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an ancient city whose marble streets once echoed with a million footsteps
clues: Colonnaded marble streets stretch toward a hillside, lined with the eroded facades of libraries, bathhouses, and temples built for gods long since forgotten.
The city once had a sophisticated sewer system, heated floors, and a library holding 12,000 scrolls — feats of engineering that vanished with the empire that built them.
Its Great Theatre, carved into the hillside, held 25,000 spectators and was where the Apostle Paul reportedly caused a riot preaching against idol worship.
Located on the Aegean coast of modern-day Turkey, it was once the second-largest city in the Roman Empire after Rome itself.

On a quiet wooded hillside above the ruins stands a small stone house that millions of pilgrims — and several visiting popes — believe to be the final home of the mother of Jesus, brought here for safekeeping by the apostle she was entrusted to at the foot of the cross.
puzzles.funFact: Ephesus had ancient 'advertisements' carved into the pavement — a footprint, a woman's face, and a heart pointing toward the city's brothel, so visiting sailors who didn't speak the language could still find their way.

photo.description: people walking in front of brown concrete building during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a misty highland park where the rarest great apes on Earth look you in the eye
clues: Dense bamboo gives way to ancient hagenia forest on a series of volcanic slopes, where mist clings to the canopy and the silence is broken only by cracking branches.

Trekkers here spend hours hiking to reach a gorilla family, then sit within metres of them for a full hour — one of the only places on Earth where sustained contact with wild great apes is a regular experience.
Dian Fossey lived and worked on these slopes for 18 years, was murdered here in 1985, and chose to be buried in the gorilla graveyard she created — among the animals she gave her life to protect.
Located in northwestern Rwanda on the slopes of the Virunga volcano chain, a single trekking permit costs $1,500 — revenue that has directly funded a rare conservation success story.

Every September, celebrities like Kevin Hart, Idris Elba and Naomi Campbell gather at the foot of these slopes for a beloved national ceremony — borrowed from a local tradition of naming newborn children — in which they give names to the baby mountain gorillas born here that year.
puzzles.funFact: Mountain gorilla numbers have actually increased in recent decades — the only great ape population currently growing — because trekking permit revenue of $1,500 per person funds anti-poaching patrols so effectively that the gorillas are safer now than at any point in the past century.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a medieval walled city cradled between dark mountains and a glassy Adriatic bay
clues: Stone walls climb the steep mountain directly behind a perfectly preserved old town, their switchbacks visible for kilometres as they ascend toward a ruined fortress.
The bay enclosing the city is so deep and sheltered it was long mistaken for a fjord — its calm water mirrors the grey limestone cliffs above.
Venetian-era palaces, Romanesque churches, and cats — hundreds of them — define the labyrinthine streets inside these ancient fortifications.

Tucked at the very head of Europe's most southerly fjord-like gulf, this small Montenegrin town spent nearly four centuries under Venetian rule and was among the first places on this coast named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Centuries ago, Venetian sailors left their ship cats behind in this Montenegrin port, and the descendants have ruled the lanes ever since — locals treat them as good-luck guardians and the town's unofficial emblem, with a dedicated cat museum and souvenir stalls in their honour.
puzzles.funFact: Kotor is so famous for its cats that the city has a dedicated Cat Museum and sells cat-themed souvenirs at nearly every stall — the animals have been considered sacred protectors of the old town since Venetian sailors brought them on ships centuries ago.

photo.description: houses near body of water during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an Inca citadel so remote that fewer people visit it in a year than Machu Picchu sees in an hour
clues: Stone terraces cascade down a mountain ridge above a roaring river canyon, the stonework precise and proud despite centuries of encroaching jungle.
The approach requires a two-day trek through dramatic mountain scenery — there is no road, no cable car, and no shortcut to this citadel.
Archaeologists estimate only 30 to 40 percent of this site has been excavated — more ruins lie under the jungle than have ever been seen by modern eyes.
Located in southern Peru near Cusco, it shares its architectural DNA with Machu Picchu — the same precision stonework and sacred alignment with the peaks above.

Set into the dark terrace walls here is a herd of pale stone llamas — more than twenty of them, complete with a little herdsman, marching up the Andean hillside in a mosaic of white rock that no other Inca site can claim.
puzzles.funFact: During the Spanish conquest, the last Inca rulers used Choquequirao as a refuge and are believed to have brought enormous quantities of gold there — which was never surrendered to the Spanish and has never been found. It may still be somewhere beneath the jungle.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the highest peak in a land of glaciers, lakes, and sky
clues: A pyramid of ice-raked rock rises above a valley of turquoise glacial rivers, its summit so frequently shrouded in cloud that local people believed it touched the sky.
On its flanks lies the Tasman Glacier — the longest glacier in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica, calving icebergs into a milky blue lake at its terminal face.
Edmund Hillary trained on these glaciers and slopes before becoming the first person to summit Everest — the mountain prepared him for everything that followed.
Located in the Southern Alps on New Zealand's South Island, it is the country's highest peak and sacred to the Māori who call it 'Cloud Piercer'.

Sir Edmund Hillary is the only non-royal ever to appear on this country's banknotes while still alive — and on the five-dollar note he stands beside the nation's highest peak, the snowy giant pictured at his shoulder.
puzzles.funFact: Aoraki Mount Cook is one of the only mountains in the world with two official names of fully equal legal standing — 'Aoraki' in Māori and 'Mount Cook' in English — after a 1998 treaty between the New Zealand government and the local iwi.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the world's largest car-free urban area — an ancient city that has barely changed in a thousand years
clues: Nine thousand narrow alleyways thread between tanneries, madrasas, and souks in a labyrinth so dense that sunlight barely reaches the cobblestones below.
The smell hits before the sight — the pungent, medieval aroma of dye, leather, and spice rising from a city that has worked the same trades for centuries.
The medina is so labyrinthine that even locals use the overlapping calls to prayer from dozens of mosques to orient themselves — sound is the city's navigation system.
Located in northern Morocco, this medina is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and home to the world's oldest continuously operating university, founded in 859 AD.

A devout immigrant woman, Fatima al-Fihri, is said to have poured her entire inheritance into building a mosque and madrasa here in 859 AD — and the institution she is credited with founding has never closed its doors since, making her the woman remembered for creating the oldest seat of learning still teaching today.
puzzles.funFact: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fes was founded in 859 AD by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri — recognised by UNESCO as the world's oldest continuously operating university, predating Oxford by over 200 years.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a landscape powered from below — where the Earth itself breathes
clues: The ground here is warm underfoot; rainbow-ringed pools of boiling water punctuate a landscape that hisses, steams, and erupts on a schedule of its own.
Bison graze at the edge of geothermal vents, seemingly indifferent to the fact that they stand above one of the largest supervolcanoes on the planet.
It is home to the largest free-roaming bison herd in North America — descendants of the last wild herd to survive the 19th-century mass slaughter that killed 60 million of them.
The world's first national park, established in 1872 in the western United States, it protects more than half of the world's geysers within its borders.

A picnic-basket-stealing cartoon bear who brags that he's "smarter than the average bear" — and his little sidekick Boo-Boo — were dreamed up by Hanna-Barbera as residents of a national park whose name is a playful rhyme on this real American one, complete with its own perpetually exasperated Ranger Smith.
puzzles.funFact: Old Faithful has been erupting for centuries and has never once missed its schedule by more than 20 minutes — the National Park Service posts predicted eruption times based on the duration of the previous eruption, a geological clock accurate enough to set your watch by.

photo.description: blue and brown water on brown rock

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a golden temple that feeds 100,000 people every single day — for free
clues: A gleaming golden structure rises from the centre of a sacred pool of still water, reached by a marble causeway where pilgrims walk barefoot through the early morning silence.
The complex runs one of the largest free kitchens on Earth — every visitor regardless of faith or status is fed without charge, day and night.
Its four doors, one facing each direction, symbolise the acceptance of all people from all corners of the world — no religion, caste, or class is turned away.
Located in Amritsar in the Punjab region of India, it is the holiest shrine of the Sikh faith and a symbol of radical equality and service.

Two centuries ago the one-eyed "Lion of Punjab," Maharaja Ranjit Singh, had its upper storeys sheathed in hundreds of kilograms of gold leaf — so today the shrine seems to float as a single shimmering island, its mirror image rippling in the still sacred lake that rings it.
puzzles.funFact: The Golden Temple's langar — community kitchen — serves free meals to between 50,000 and 100,000 people every single day, run entirely by volunteers and donations. It has never once closed in its history, including during wars and pandemics.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city that produces more hot spring water than anywhere else on Earth — a place where the ground itself is alive
clues: Steam rises from drains, pavements, and roadside vents throughout this city — an almost permanent mist that gives even ordinary streets an otherworldly quality.
Its eight geothermal pools — known locally as the 'Hells' — range from blood-red to brilliant cobalt blue, each a different mineral composition, each at near-boiling point.
The city produces over 130,000 tonnes of hot spring water every day — more than any other city on Earth — used for cooking, bathing, heating homes, and even cooking eggs in the steam.
Located on the island of Kyushu in Japan, it has been a pilgrimage destination for hot spring bathers for over a thousand years.

Visitors here are famously buried up to the neck in hot black sand on the beach, gazing at the sea while the ground steams them like a kettle — then warm up in a town so thick with scalding, jewel-coloured volcanic ponds that columns of steam rise from its streets all day long.
puzzles.funFact: Beppu residents cook food using nothing but geothermal steam — a local tradition called 'jigoku mushi' (hell steaming) that uses the city's natural heat to prepare vegetables, eggs, and even puddings in wooden steamers placed directly over ground vents.

photo.description: gray rocks on body of water

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a plateau scattered with thousands of ancient stone vessels whose purpose remains a mystery
clues: Thousands of enormous stone cylinders — some taller than a person and weighing several tonnes — are scattered across a highland plateau like discarded cups of giants.
They were carved over 2,000 years ago by a civilisation that left no written records — their purpose is still debated: funeral urns, rice wine vats, or rainwater collectors.
The plateau around them is pocked with bomb craters — this landscape was one of the most heavily bombed places on Earth during the 1960s, and unexploded ordnance still makes some sites off-limits.
Located in Xieng Khouang province in northern Laos, the site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2019.

During a secret war run alongside the Vietnam conflict, this remote corner of Southeast Asia became the most heavily bombed place on Earth per person in history — more tonnage fell here than was dropped in all of World War II, and clearance teams still defuse the unexploded leftovers scattered between the ancient stone vessels today.
puzzles.funFact: Laos is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history — the US dropped more bombs on it during the Vietnam War era than on all of Europe in World War II combined, and an estimated 30% of them never exploded and still kill people today.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a volcanic lake so beautiful that Aldous Huxley called it 'the most beautiful lake in the world'
clues: Three towering volcanoes preside over a deep caldera lake, their reflections trembling in water that shifts from brilliant blue to silver depending on the hour.
A dozen indigenous Maya villages cling to its shores, each with its own distinct textile traditions and Mayan dialect, reachable only by motorboat across the shimmering water.
The lake has no natural outlet — it drains entirely through porous volcanic rock — and its depth has never been reliably measured, with estimates ranging from 200 to over 340 metres.
Located in the Guatemalan Highlands of Central America at 1,562 metres elevation, it is considered sacred by the surrounding Maya communities and formed by a supervolcanic eruption 84,000 years ago.

In the 1990s a local diver descended into these blue-green Guatemalan highland depths and found an entire sunken Maya city — temples, plazas and stone altars swallowed when the water rose roughly 1,800 years ago, earning it the nickname "the Maya Atlantis."
puzzles.funFact: Divers exploring Lake Atitlán's floor have found submerged ancient Maya ruins — temples and ceremonial structures flooded when the lake level rose, now visible only to those who descend into the blue-green depths.

photo.description: a dock leading out to a boat in the water with Lake Atitlán in the background

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a Silk Road city so intact it feels like time stopped five centuries ago
clues: Terracotta walls encircle a compact maze of mosques, minarets, and madrasas, all in the same sandy palette as the desert surrounding them on every side.
The main minaret here was never completed — it was intended to be the tallest in the region, but the emir died before it reached its planned height and no one dared finish it.
Families inside the inner walled city trace their ancestry directly to the Silk Road merchants and craftsmen who lived here centuries ago — the same trades, the same streets, the same families.
Located in the Khorezm region of Uzbekistan, near the Amu Darya River that once fed the now-vanishing Aral Sea, it was a key trading post on the ancient Silk Road.

Behind its mud-brick walls, this desert city ran Central Asia's most notorious open-air slave bazaar — captives seized by Turkmen raiders were displayed for sale in niches built into the long passage of the inner city's eastern gate. When the Russian army stormed the khanate in 1873, it forced the ruler to free his slaves on the spot, liberating tens of thousands of Persians in a single stroke.
puzzles.funFact: Khiva's Kalta Minor minaret was supposed to be visible from Bukhara, 500 km away — an architectural ego trip cut short when the commissioning emir died, and the project stopped forever, leaving a wide, squat stump that is now the city's most recognisable structure.

photo.description: A narrow street with a tall building in the background

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the city where Africa and Brazil fused to create a culture unlike anywhere else on Earth
clues: Brightly coloured colonial buildings line the cobblestones of a hilltop old town overlooking a vast bay — the largest in the Americas — where the Atlantic light is extraordinary at every hour.
The music here is inescapable — percussion-heavy, syncopated rhythms born from three centuries of African influence that permeate the streets, bars, and churches in equal measure.
It was the first capital of a great colonial empire and the port through which more enslaved Africans arrived than any other city in the Americas — a history that shaped every aspect of its culture.
Located on a peninsula in the state of Bahia in northeastern Brazil, its historic centre Pelourinho is a UNESCO World Heritage Site of vivid Portuguese colonial and Afro-Brazilian architecture.

Brazil's best-loved novelist set his most famous story here — the sensual comedy of a widow visited by her dead husband's lusty ghost, filmed in the city's old quarter with Sônia Braga and, for 35 years, the biggest box-office hit in the nation's history.
puzzles.funFact: More enslaved Africans arrived in Salvador than in any other city in the Americas — over 1.5 million people — which is why Salvador today has the largest African-descended population outside Africa, and why its food, music, religion, and dance are more African than Portuguese.

photo.description: a group of people that are standing in the street

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a medieval Flemish city so preserved that film directors use it as a real-life movie set
clues: Stepped gable houses in ochre, brick red, and pale gold line a network of calm canals, their reflections shimmering below carved stone bridges.
Swans drift past chocolate shops and breweries in a city whose entire medieval centre has barely changed in 600 years.
It was once the trading capital of northern Europe — ships from Venice, Genoa, and England docked here before the harbour silted up and commerce moved elsewhere.
Located in the Flanders region of Belgium, its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the finest examples of Flemish Gothic architecture anywhere.

In a beloved 2008 black comedy, Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson play two hitmen ordered to lie low in this fairy-tale Belgian town — one is enchanted by its canals, cobbled squares and medieval belfry, while the other spends the whole film grumbling that it's the most boring place on Earth. The film is named simply for the town they're stuck in.
puzzles.funFact: For four centuries after trade collapsed, Bruges was too economically depressed to afford renovation — no developer wanted to invest, no city council had funds to modernise. Poverty turned out to be the most effective preservation policy in history.

photo.description: a group of buildings next to a body of water with Bruges in the background

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a smouldering crater rising from a sea of sand in the middle of a vast volcanic caldera
clues: A perfectly conical volcano, its crater rim wreathed in sulphurous smoke, rises from a pale grey 'sea of sand' — a flat ash plain stretching to the encircling caldera walls.
The ash plain surrounding it is so otherworldly that horses are hired to carry visitors across it — a surreal procession of riders dwarfed by the smoking mountain ahead.
The Tenggerese people have lived on the slopes of this active volcano for centuries and have never left — they believe the mountain is their ancestor and that it will never harm them.
Located in East Java, Indonesia, it sits within the Tengger Caldera — a collapsed ancient supervolcano — and remains one of the country's most visited and most active volcanoes.

Marooned in the middle of its black volcanic sand desert stands a lone Hindu temple of dark stone — the only structure for miles — where, in this overwhelmingly Muslim country, worshippers still climb to the crater's edge and cast offerings of livestock, fruit and money into the smoking mouth to thank their gods.
puzzles.funFact: During the Yadnya Kasada festival, the Tenggerese throw live chickens, vegetables, and money into the active volcanic crater as offerings — and locals scramble down the inner slopes trying to catch the offerings before they fall in, believing anything caught carries the mountain's blessing.

photo.description: brown mountain under white clouds during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a Baltic walled city so perfectly preserved it looks like a film set for the Middle Ages
clues: Conical towers and stepped gable rooftops rise behind a ring of medieval walls, the old city perched on a limestone plateau above a deep natural harbour.
Cobbled alleyways between sandstone and limestone buildings lead to a hilltop cathedral and the ramparts of a 13th-century fortress — all in continuous use today.
The old town survived Soviet occupation completely intact — modernisation programmes that transformed every other major Baltic city somehow left this one untouched.
The capital of Estonia, on the Baltic Sea, it was a Hanseatic League city — one of a network of prosperous medieval trading ports stretching from London to Novgorod.

In a Soviet-era building in this same city — a former cybernetics institute — a handful of local engineers wrote the software that let the world make free calls over the internet: Skype. The tiny digital-first nation it crowns now lets citizens vote and file taxes entirely online.
puzzles.funFact: Tallinn's Town Hall Pharmacy has been operating continuously since 1422 — over 600 years — making it one of the oldest pharmacies in the world still serving customers from the same address.

photo.description: An aerial view of a city with a church tower

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the largest ancient religious complex ever built — added to by 30 consecutive pharaohs over 2,000 years
clues: A forest of columns nearly 20 metres tall fills a hall so vast that Notre-Dame Cathedral could fit inside it with room to spare — and this is just one room in a complex of dozens.
It took over 2,000 years and 30 consecutive rulers to build — each adding their own hall, obelisk, or statue, each competing to outdo the previous dynasty in scale and grandeur.
Every pharaoh who built here also chiselled out their predecessor's name and replaced it with their own — the entire complex is a monument to three millennia of competitive royal ego.
Located near Luxor on the east bank of the Nile in Egypt, it was the most important place of worship in the ancient Egyptian world for over two thousand years.

In a 1970s James Bond film, Roger Moore's 007 fought the steel-toothed henchman Jaws among these towering ancient stone columns — toppling the scaffolding to bury him, then walking off with the dry quip "Egyptian builders," never realising the giant would simply climb out and keep coming.
puzzles.funFact: Karnak's sacred lake has been continuously full of water for over 3,000 years — fed by groundwater seeping from the Nile — a feat of ancient hydraulic engineering that still works perfectly today without any modern maintenance.

photo.description: a row of statues in front of a brick wall

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to the world's most accessible active volcano — where you can stand at the rim and watch the Earth roar
clues: The glow is visible from the ocean at night — a smouldering summit that hurls incandescent rocks into the air dozens of times a day, reliably, like clockwork.
Unlike most active volcanoes, a dirt track leads almost to the summit — visitors walk the final slope on foot and reach the crater edge where the lava lake erupts every few minutes.
It has been erupting continuously for at least 800 years — one of the longest documented continuous eruptions on Earth — and the local indigenous people consider it their ancestral god.
Located on the island of Tanna in the Pacific archipelago nation of Vanuatu, it is one of the most visited attractions in Melanesia.

A remote tribe on this volcano's island worships the late husband of Britain's longest-reigning queen as a living god — believing him to be the pale-skinned son of their mountain spirit, foretold to sail to a distant land, wed a powerful woman, and one day return; when he died in 2021 they declared weeks of mourning, marked by ritual wailing and ceremonial dance.
puzzles.funFact: Captain Cook spotted Mount Yasur's glow from the sea in 1774 and used it to navigate by night — making it the first volcano in the Pacific to be recorded by a European explorer, over 250 years ago.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city of 15 million where the call to prayer has echoed across seven hills for a thousand years
clues: Minarets and domes puncture a skyline stretching across seven hills above a famous strait — a city whose silhouette has defined the imagination of travellers since antiquity.
The call to prayer from hundreds of mosques echoes here across a metropolis of 15 million that has been capital of both the Roman and the Ottoman empires.
A covered bazaar here contains over 4,000 shops under one roof — in continuous operation since 1461 and receiving up to 400,000 visitors a day.
Its history spans three successive empires — Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman — each leaving layers of architecture that coexist in the same streets and skyline.
Located in Turkey, this city straddles the Bosphorus strait — the only major city in the world where half sits in Europe and half in Asia, with millions crossing between continents daily.
puzzles.funFact: Istanbul is the only city in the world that sits on two continents — its European and Asian halves are connected by three suspension bridges and two undersea rail tunnels, with millions of people crossing between continents on their daily commute.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a city that reinvents itself completely every winter
clues: Each January, a flat field beside a frozen river is transformed into an illuminated city of palaces, pagodas, and cathedrals — every structure glowing from within against a −30°C sky.
Temperatures here regularly plunge below −30°C during construction, when thousands of workers spend weeks carving ice into architectural forms up to 50 metres tall.
The festival grew from a simple local tradition of ice lanterns into the world's largest snow and ice festival, attracting over a million visitors in a single season.
Located in Heilongjiang province in northeastern China near the Russian border, it draws blocks of ice cut directly from the frozen Songhua River.

Built a century ago by Russian railway engineers and then flooded with White Russians fleeing the Bolsheviks, this Chinese city filled with onion-domed Orthodox cathedrals — earning it the nickname "the Moscow of the East" — and that long love affair with deep northern winters is exactly what its dazzling festival of carved, glowing ice now celebrates.
puzzles.funFact: The ice blocks used at Harbin are cut from the Songhua River in complete darkness at 3am, when the ice is thickest and clearest — each block is inspected for transparency before being hoisted by crane onto the building site.

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to an island city where Arab, Persian, Indian, and African cultures fused into something entirely its own
clues: Carved wooden doors studded with brass spikes line the narrow streets of an old town where the architecture blends Islamic arches, Indian balconies, and Swahili craftsmanship.
The smell of cloves, cardamom, and coconut drifts through the alleyways — this island once supplied the world with the majority of its spice crop.
An Anglican cathedral stands directly over the site of the last open-air slave market in East Africa — a deliberate act of memorial where the altar stands where the whipping post once was.

In 1840 an Omani sultan was so taken with this Indian Ocean trading island that he shifted his entire court here from Muscat, ruling his Arabian empire from African shores until a mid-19th-century succession split severed the two halves for good.

The flamboyant frontman of Queen was born here as Farrokh Bulsara, and his family fled the island's 1964 revolution for England — today a museum tucked down one of the old town's lanes honours the rock legend the world came to know as Freddie Mercury.
puzzles.funFact: Freddie Mercury was born in Zanzibar Stone Town in 1946 as Farrokh Bulsara — the island now has a dedicated museum in his honour, though he left as a child and spoke very little about his origins during his lifetime.

photo.description: aerial photography of village near body of water

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to a volcanic island where female divers still harvest the sea floor by hand — some in their 80s
clues: A dormant shield volcano dominates the centre of an island whose lava tubes, black beaches, and tangerine orchards give it a landscape unlike anything else in its region.
The island is famous for its haenyeo — women divers, some in their 70s and 80s, who hold their breath and dive to the sea floor to harvest abalone and sea urchin by hand.
It has its own dialect incomprehensible to mainland speakers, its own UNESCO Intangible Heritage traditions, and its own set of creation myths involving giants who built the island.
Located off the southern tip of South Korea, it is the country's largest island and most popular domestic holiday destination, often called the 'Hawaii of Korea'.

For decades it WAS the honeymoon: back when Cold War rules barred ordinary citizens from flying abroad, newlyweds took the one-hour hop from Seoul to this warm volcanic island in such numbers that the national railway ran a dedicated 'honeymoon train' to ferry couples on their way.
puzzles.funFact: Because haenyeo women were the primary breadwinners in Jeju households for centuries, Jeju developed an unusually matriarchal social structure — men stayed home, raised children, and did housework while grandmothers dove to 20 metres to feed the family.

photo.description: cliff near body of water during daytime

puzzles.teaser: Tomorrow's quest takes you to one of the most desolate and dramatic coastlines on Earth — where the desert meets the fog and the ocean claims what it will
clues: A beach of black rock and rusted shipwrecks stretches into a grey murk so thick it erases the horizon — the ocean and the desert merge in eerie, impenetrable silence.
Hundreds of Cape fur seals haul themselves onto the shore, their barking audible from kilometres away, while jackals and brown hyenas patrol the colony edges.
Sailors who survived wrecks here rarely survived what came next — an unbroken desert with no freshwater for hundreds of kilometres in every direction.
Located along the northern coast of Namibia bordering Angola, it was named by the Bushmen 'The Land God Made in Anger' — and by Portuguese sailors 'The Gates of Hell'.

A German cargo ship that ran aground here in thick fog over a century ago now sits half-buried nearly half a kilometre from the water — the desert advances so relentlessly that the dunes have swallowed the wreck and left the sea behind.
puzzles.funFact: Over 1,000 ships have wrecked on the Skeleton Coast — the cold Benguela Current, dense fog, and violent surf made it one of the most dangerous stretches of ocean on Earth, and survivors who reached shore faced an unbroken desert with no water in any direction.

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast open gravel-and-grass meadow ringed by city streets, with a colossal bronze female figure and a crouching lion standing on a low hill before a long Doric-columned hall of fame, the spires of a southern German city rising in the haze beyond.
clues: Roughly six to seven million people pour onto this single 42-hectare meadow over about 16 days each year, making it host to the largest folk festival on Earth.
The whole tradition began as a public party for an 1810 royal wedding: a crown prince married his princess, and the field was christened in her honor, the name it still carries today.

After the wedding races proved wildly popular, citizens were invited back the next year and the next, and a five-day celebration slowly grew into an annual institution that spread its name around the world.
On a hilltop at one edge of this southern German meadow stands a colossal bronze woman in a bearskin, an oak wreath, and a lion at her feet, gazing out from beside a Doric-columned hall of fame.

Climb the spiral stair hidden inside that 18-metre statue and you can peer out through openings in her helmet at the crowds below; her king boasted that only he and the emperor Nero could cast giants so large.
puzzles.funFact: The hollow bronze colossus overlooking the grounds was the first monumental statue cast entirely in bronze since classical antiquity, and a spiral staircase climbs up inside her body to a tiny viewing room in her head.
puzzles.teaser: A wedding toast from 1810 that two centuries later still spills across a meadow in millions of liters.

photo.description: Amusement park with tower and stalls

puzzles.imageDescription: A blinding-white cracked clay pan stretches flat under a hard blue sky, studded with the black, leafless skeletons of long-dead trees. Behind them, vast rust-orange sand dunes rise like a wall, their knife-edge ridges glowing in the low sun.
clues: The blackened trees scattered across this dazzling white floor have stood without leaves for roughly six centuries, kept from rotting because the air around them is simply too dry for decay.

Photographers call it a place where time stopped: the lifeless trunks against pale clay and burning dunes have made it one of the most copied desert images on Earth, a staple of camera-club bucket lists.
It was born when a river that once flooded this hollow shifted its course; the marsh-loving trees that had taken root were left to wither as encroaching sand sealed off the water for good.
It sits inside the oldest desert on the planet, a strip of southwestern Africa parched for tens of millions of years, where some of the tallest dunes anywhere wall in a cracked clay basin.
Climbers haul themselves up the towering ridge nicknamed for a 'big' patriarch, then run down its flank to reach the ghostly grove of camelthorn skeletons frozen on the glaring pan below.
puzzles.funFact: The dead camelthorn trees aren't petrified or fossilized at all - they're just bone-dry wood. The Namib's hyper-arid air has prevented them from decomposing for around 600 years, so they're essentially natural mummies still standing where they died.
puzzles.teaser: Where dead trees refuse to fall, and the desert turns the floor to bone.

photo.description: withered trees under clear blue sky

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast stone terrace at the foot of a barren mountain, scattered with slender fluted columns and a monumental gateway flanked by colossal human-headed winged bulls. Long ceremonial staircases are carved with rows of figures in procession, glowing honey-gold in the dry sunlight.
clues: This UNESCO-listed terrace city, raised on a vast stone platform against a mountainside, became one of the wealthiest places on earth before it was looted of treasures said to need thousands of pack animals to carry away.

Legend says that after a drunken banquet, a courtesan urged a young conqueror to set the palace ablaze in revenge for an earlier burning of her homeland's temples, and the great halls went up in flames.
Founded as a ceremonial capital by a king who called himself King of Kings, it was begun around 515 BC and expanded by his son and grandson over many decades of construction.

Its great audience hall staircase is carved with delegates from 23 subject peoples bringing tribute, and the site sat at the heart of an empire whose heartland lies in the south of modern Iran, near present-day Shiraz.

Each spring the kings here received the homage of their realm during the new-year festival, and a monumental gateway still guards the approach, its doorways watched over by colossal human-headed winged bulls.
puzzles.funFact: When Alexander's army torched the palaces in 330 BC, the fire baked thousands of clay administrative tablets in the treasury archive, accidentally preserving them; they survive today and record the wages paid to the workers who built the city.
puzzles.teaser: A king of kings raised it in stone, and a single banquet brought it down in fire.

photo.description: architectural photography gray monument

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast red-sandstone mosque with three swelling white marble domes and four tall octagonal minarets framing an immense empty courtyard, glowing warm against a hazy sky at golden hour.
clues: For more than three centuries after it opened, no mosque on Earth was larger; its open courtyard alone can hold around 100,000 worshippers, and it kept that world record until a modern rival was finished in the 1980s.
A reclusive local family later gifted it a chamber of sacred relics said to include a turban, strands of hair, and a robe attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, kept above the main gateway.

An emperor raised it in barely two years in the early 1670s to celebrate his military campaigns deep in the south against a rising Maratha power, the last truly great monument of his dynasty's mosque-building.
It rises directly across from a great fort in this South Asian country's cultural capital, its glowing red sandstone trimmed with white marble inlay and crowned by three bulbous marble domes.
Conquering soldiers once stabled their cavalry horses in its sweeping courtyard and packed gunpowder into the cells along its walls, a humiliation before it was finally restored to prayer.
puzzles.funFact: The four main minarets stand about 60 metres (196 ft) tall, and during the 19th-century Sikh occupation the emperor's grand courtyard was used as a stable for army horses while its surrounding cells became gunpowder magazines.
puzzles.teaser: Red stone and white marble, raised in two years to crown an empire at its zenith.

photo.description: brown concrete building under blue sky during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A towering vermilion wooden gate with six legs and a curved double crossbeam stands directly in shallow tidal water, its reflection rippling on the sea at high tide. Behind it, a wooden shrine complex on stilts hugs the shoreline beneath forested green mountains.
clues: At high tide this giant vermilion gate appears to float on the open sea, yet it is anchored by nothing but its own roughly 60-ton weight — it simply rests on the seabed rather than being buried in it.

A powerful 12th-century warlord and naval clan chief rebuilt this sanctuary in the elegant courtly style of his era, and his clan later staged grand boat rituals here that survive as one of the nation's great water festivals.

The site has been venerated for well over a thousand years, but it was that warlord-governor's 1168 reconstruction that gave it the over-the-water layout famous today; the gate's distinctive six-legged form dates to the 16th century and the present structure to 1875.

It sits on a sacred forested island in an inland sea of this country, where the ground was once held so pure that, even now, births and burials on the island are forbidden and free-roaming deer wander the shrine approaches.

The whole complex was raised on stilts like a pier so that pilgrims could worship without defiling the holy island with their footsteps — its twin main pillars carved from single 500-year-old camphor trunks, naturally resistant to rot in the salt water.
puzzles.funFact: The great gate isn't planted into the seabed at all — it stands purely by its own weight, with about 7 tons of fist-sized stones packed into the hollow upper crossbeam to ballast it against the tides and typhoons.
puzzles.teaser: A crimson gate adrift on the tide, guarding an island too sacred to be born or buried on.

photo.description: red shrine in body of water

puzzles.imageDescription: Two gleaming stainless-steel and glass spires soar side by side against a tropical sky, joined high in the air by a slender double-decker walkway. The faceted facades taper into pointed pinnacles, and the matching towers mirror each other above a busy city center.
clues: For six years around the turn of the millennium, these were the tallest buildings on Earth, and they remain the tallest matched pair of their kind anywhere in the world.
A 1999 caper film starred an aging master thief and his accomplice rappelling from the slender walkway between them in the climactic escape, cementing the structure's pop-culture fame.
Construction began in 1993, the gleaming pinnacles topped out in 1996, and the prime minister officially opened the complex on the nation's independence day in 1999.
Rising over a Southeast Asian capital famous for its night markets and roti canai, the floorplan is built on an eight-pointed star drawn from Islamic art, honoring the country's Muslim faith.
Halfway up, a two-level bridge links the pair on the 41st and 42nd floors, about 170 meters above the street, and it can detach to slide rather than snap if the towers sway.
puzzles.funFact: The double-decker skybridge isn't rigidly bolted to the towers; it sits on sliding bearings so it can move independently as the two towers sway in the wind, preventing it from snapping.
puzzles.teaser: Twin silver spires, joined by a bridge in the sky.

photo.description: Petronas Tower

puzzles.imageDescription: A near-perfect, isolated rock pyramid with a steeply pitched, hooked summit, its four sheer faces rising over alpine meadows and glaciers under a crisp blue sky.
clues: Though far from the tallest peak in its range, this lone 4,478-meter pyramid is one of the most photographed mountains on Earth, its silhouette stamped onto a famous triangular chocolate bar.
Its 1865 first ascent ended in tragedy: on the descent a climber slipped, a weak rope snapped, and four of the seven-man party plunged thousands of feet to a glacier below.
For centuries locals believed it unclimbable and even cursed; the deadly race to its summit pitted rival teams climbing from two different countries against each other.
It straddles the frontier between Valais in Switzerland and Italy's Aosta Valley, towering over the car-free resort village reached only by train.

Three of its four sheer faces drain into one country and the fourth into another, so a guide leading you up the famous ridge can have you cross an international border without a single road or checkpoint.
puzzles.funFact: The mountain's image on Toblerone bars hides a rearing bear in the rock face, a nod to Bern, the chocolate's home city, whose symbol is the bear.
puzzles.teaser: A lonely stone pyramid that became the logo of an entire mountain range.

photo.description: snow covered mountain under blue sky during night time

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast neo-Gothic riverfront palace bristling with pinnacles and a soaring central dome, mirrored in the dark water of a great river at dusk, its honey-colored stone facade lit golden against the twilight sky.
clues: Its skyline bristles with exactly 365 towers and spires, one for every day of the year, and its lavish interior swallowed roughly 40 kilograms of gold.
Since the dawn of the year 2000 it has guarded a sacred relic under its central dome: the millennium-old crowning jewel of the nation's first king and saint.
Work began in 1885 to honor the country's thousandth birthday; its visionary architect reportedly went blind and died before the building he dreamed up was finally finished in 1904.
It rises 96 meters above a famous river's eastern bank in this Central European capital, a height chosen to echo the year 896 and matched exactly by the city's great basilica.
A red communist star once crowned its dome until it was stripped away in 1990, and at 268 meters long it remains the largest parliament building on its continent.
puzzles.funFact: By a long-standing rule, no building in the capital was permitted to rise above 96 meters, so this riverfront palace and the city's grand basilica share the exact same height to symbolize the balance of worldly and spiritual power.
puzzles.teaser: A thousand-year crown sleeps beneath a dome of 365 spires, glowing above a dark river.

photo.description: brown concrete building near body of water during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A towering green-patinated copper figure of a robed woman stands on a star-shaped stone pedestal on a small island, raising a torch toward the sky with a tablet cradled in her other arm, set against open harbor water and a distant skyline.
clues: She arrived by ship from across the Atlantic disassembled into roughly 350 separate pieces packed in over 200 crates, then was bolted back together on her own island.
A famous sonnet calling her the "Mother of Exiles" was written to help fund her base, and its lines about huddled masses yearning to breathe free are now mounted at her feet.
Conceived after the American Civil War as a joint gift between two republics, her broken chains and shackles were meant to honor newly won freedom and emancipation.
She rises from a tiny island in a harbor in the northeastern United States, the first sight that greeted millions of immigrants arriving by sea into a great port city.

Her copper skin is barely thicker than two coins, draped over a hidden iron skeleton engineered by the same Frenchman who would soon raise a wrought-iron tower over Paris; in her tablet she holds the Roman-numeral date of a 1776 declaration.
puzzles.funFact: Her green color is not paint but a natural patina: the originally shiny copper-brown statue slowly oxidized over about three decades, and by the 1920s had turned the familiar blue-green seen today.
puzzles.teaser: A copper giant who crossed an ocean in pieces to light the way home for the weary.

photo.description: city skyline across body of water during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A near-conical granite peak rising straight out of the deep blue water at the mouth of a wide bay, ringed by a glass-walled aerial cable car gliding between stations, with a sprawling coastal city and forested hills spread out far below.
clues: When its aerial tramway opened in 1912 it was only the third cable car of its kind ever built anywhere on Earth, a daring engineering gamble strung between two rocky summits.
In a 1979 spy blockbuster, the steel-toothed henchman 'Jaws' famously gnaws through the tramway cable in a mid-air brawl atop one of these very cars; the prop cable was actually made of liquorice.
Portuguese sailors named it in the 16th century because its smooth, near-conical shape reminded them of the clay molds used to ship refined blocks of colonial sugar.
It is a near-bare gneiss-and-granite monolith standing guard at the entrance to Guanabara Bay, soaring straight out of the Atlantic beside one of South America's most famous coastlines.

Visitors ride two glass gondolas in sequence, pausing at a lower forested hump before the final lift to a 396-metre summit that looks back over a crescent beach district and a giant hilltop statue across the water.
puzzles.funFact: For the Moonraker cable-car fight, the steel cable that 'Jaws' bites through was actually made of liquorice, though actor Richard Kiel still wore his real steel dentures for the close-up.
puzzles.teaser: A bare stone thumb at the harbor mouth, where a glass car climbs into the clouds.

photo.description: cliff in middle of body of water during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast turquoise and cobalt mosaic of coral structures threaded by deep blue channels, fringed by pale sandy cays, photographed from high above where the living reef bleeds into the open sea.
clues: It is the largest living structure on the planet, an interlinked system of roughly 2,900 reefs and 900 islands so immense it can be picked out from low Earth orbit.
A small, naturally heart-shaped coral formation here has become a legendary spot for marriage proposals, glimpsed only from a scenic helicopter or seaplane flyover.
What you see today is geologically young: the modern reef colonized a drowned continental shelf only after the last Ice Age, as melting ice flooded the lowlands some 8,000 to 10,000 years ago.
It runs for more than 2,300 kilometres along the warm Coral Sea edge of a single state on a southern-hemisphere continent, sheltering six of the world's seven sea turtle species.

Inscribed as one of the planet's first natural World Heritage sites in 1981, it now battles mass coral bleaching driven by warming seas — a slow-motion crisis playing out across an area about the size of Japan.
puzzles.funFact: The Heart Reef is so delicate that snorkelling, diving and anchoring are all banned there — the only way couples can experience it is by air, which is exactly why it became a marriage-proposal flyover.
puzzles.teaser: The largest living thing on Earth, sprawling beneath a tropical sea.

photo.description: Aerial view of a heart-shaped coral reef formation

puzzles.imageDescription: Massive curving granite walls of dark, weathered dry-stacked blocks rise up to 11 metres, encircling a grassy interior dotted with smaller enclosures and a mysterious solid conical tower. The mortarless masonry glows golden-brown under an open southern-African sky, framed by scrubby hills.
clues: Its largest curving wall stands about 11 metres tall and stretches roughly 252 metres around, making it the biggest ancient stone structure anywhere in Africa south of the Sahara.
When 19th-century European visitors first saw it, they refused to believe local hands had built it and invented myths of Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba to explain it away.

Ancestors of a Bantu farming people began raising it in the 11th century, stacking precisely shaped granite blocks entirely without mortar; the city flourished for over 300 years before being abandoned around the 15th century.
It sits on the high inland plateau of southern Africa between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, in a country whose very name comes from a local phrase meaning 'houses of stone'.
Diggers here unearthed Chinese porcelain, Persian glass beads, and coins from the Swahili coast beside eight carved soapstone birds; one of those birds now perches on the modern national flag.
puzzles.funFact: When the modern nation gained independence in 1980 it took its name from this site, and a soapstone bird excavated from the ruins became the country's national emblem, appearing on its flag, coat of arms, coins, and banknotes.
puzzles.teaser: A king's stone city that traded with distant empires, then fell silent.

photo.description: a rocky hillside with a stone wall

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast white marble prayer complex crowned by 82 gleaming domes and ringed by slender minarets, its reflecting pools mirroring the facade at dusk while floral inlays of semi-precious stone wind across the courtyard floor.
clues: Beneath its main prayer hall lies a single hand-knotted carpet so enormous - over 5,600 square metres and more than two billion knots - that it holds the record as the largest in the world.
It was the dream of a nation's founding father, who wanted a place uniting the Islamic world's diversity; he died in 2004, three years before it opened, and now rests in a tomb within its grounds.

Construction stretched across more than a decade, finishing in 2007, and drew artisans and materials from dozens of countries - marble, gold, and millions of Swarovski crystals set into its chandeliers.
It rises in the capital of a Gulf federation on the Arabian Peninsula, a city of oil wealth where a sea of white domes and reflecting pools sits beside the desert.

Its courtyard floor is paved with one of the largest marble mosaics on earth, a carpet of vines and blossoms in semi-precious stone, and at night its outer walls shift color to follow the phases of the moon.
puzzles.funFact: The mosque's exterior lighting system is designed to mimic the lunar cycle: the facade glows in cooler blue-white tones that grow brighter as the moon waxes and dimmer as it wanes.
puzzles.teaser: A sea of white domes mirrored in still water, where the desert meets a galaxy of crystal.

photo.description: blue and beige concrete mosque

puzzles.imageDescription: A colossal whitewashed dome rising from a tiered mandala base, crowned by a gilded square tower painted with a pair of enormous unblinking eyes that gaze outward in every direction. Strings of multicolored prayer flags radiate from the golden spire, and a ring of pilgrims circles the base clockwise, spinning rows of brass prayer wheels.
clues: One of the largest spherical stupas on Earth, its entire ground plan is laid out as a giant three-dimensional mandala, a sacred cosmic diagram you can walk around.
A single painted symbol between the towering eyes looks like a question mark but is actually the local numeral 'one' — a reminder that there is one path to enlightenment.

Newar chronicles hint at a shrine here as far back as the 5th century, though the monument you see today was most likely raised around the 14th century over relics said to belong to a buddha of a past age.

After a 1959 uprising sent waves of refugees fleeing across the Himalayas, more than 50 monasteries sprang up around this dome, making it the beating heart of Tibetan Buddhism beyond Tibet — yet it stands in the Kathmandu Valley.

When a 2015 quake cracked its spire, devotees rebuilt the crown using over 30 kilograms of gold and 2.1 million dollars in private donations, reopening it the following year as pilgrims again spun the wheels at its base.
