puzzles.funFact: After the 2015 Nepal earthquake cracked its spire, the stupa's crown was rebuilt entirely with private donations from Buddhist groups and volunteers, using more than 30 kilograms of gold, and it reopened on 22 November 2016.
puzzles.teaser: Painted eyes on a white dome watch the four directions while pilgrims circle, spinning wheels of prayer.

photo.description: a very tall building with a lot of flags on top of it

puzzles.imageDescription: Rank upon rank of life-size clay warriors stand at attention in long earthen trenches beneath a vast hangar-like roof, their grey-brown faces each subtly different, frozen mid-march in formation.
clues: More than 8,000 life-size figures wait here in battle formation, and after decades of excavation no two faces have ever been found exactly alike.

When farmers first cracked open the buried ranks, the surviving mineral paint -- including a synthetic purple unknown elsewhere in the ancient world -- curled and flaked away within minutes of touching the dry air.
An emperor who unified warring states and standardized their script, money, and roads ordered this silent army built to guard him in death, facing east toward the lands he had conquered.
Lie in the Wei River valley of this country's Shaanxi province, just east of an ancient walled capital, beside a great earthen burial mound that has never been fully opened.
In the spring of 1974, men digging a well struck fragments of hardened clay -- one of them later spent his old age signing autographs beside the very ranks his shovel had unearthed.
puzzles.funFact: Each warrior was assembled from mass-produced parts -- legs, torsos, arms, heads -- but craftsmen then hand-carved the features, so the 8,000-strong army is effectively a gallery of thousands of individual portraits.
puzzles.teaser: An emperor's clay legions, summoned from the earth to stand guard for two thousand years.

photo.description: Terracotta soldiers

puzzles.imageDescription: Vast emerald amphitheater of stepped paddies climbing a steep mountainside in tight, hand-carved contours, with mud-and-stone retaining walls, thin irrigation channels glinting between the levels, and mist hanging over the high ridgelines above clustered farming huts.
clues: Locals call this the Eighth Wonder of the World, and the boast has math behind it: lined end to end, these stepped fields would reach roughly halfway around the planet, about 20,000 kilometers.
It is one of the very few farms in the world to appear on a nation's money, printed on the back of banknotes beside a small native palm civet and an indigenous mountain weave.

Carved into the slopes largely by hand with the simplest of tools, the terraces are said to be around two thousand years old, shaped by an upland people for irrigated rice long before modern engineering.
Hidden in the Cordillera highlands of a Southeast Asian island nation, the fields sit some 1,500 meters up, tended for generations by the Ifugao, whose ancestors first cut the steps.

Farmers here still plant a prized heirloom grain in pond-fields fed by mountain springs, climbing earthen stairways between levels in a living landscape passed down through countless generations of one upland tribe.
puzzles.funFact: Although they appear on the back of the Philippine 20-peso note and are nicknamed the Eighth Wonder of the World, the Banaue terraces themselves are not the inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Site; that 1995 listing covers five other Ifugao terrace clusters nearby, such as Batad and Bangaan.
puzzles.teaser: A green staircase climbing into the clouds, cut by hand before history was written down.

photo.description: a view of a rice field with mountains in the background

puzzles.imageDescription: An ornate ivory-white limestone tower with delicate lacework battlements, ribbed turrets and a riverside bastion, rising directly from the water's edge under a soft Atlantic light, its carved balconies and rope-twist stonework glowing against a pale sky.
clues: Tucked into the stonework of this riverside fort is what is widely considered the first sculpted likeness of a rhinoceros in Western architecture, weathered now but carved from the memory of an exotic beast that astonished a royal court.

For generations of mariners pushing off into uncharted oceans, this elegant bastion was the very last piece of homeland they saw shrinking on the horizon, and the first to greet them if they ever returned.

Begun in 1514 by a military architect already famous for North African strongholds, it was raised to guard a great river mouth and to celebrate a sea captain's recent triumph in reaching India by ship.
Its frothy, lace-like carving belongs to a lavish ornamental style found almost nowhere outside this single Atlantic-facing nation, born during a boom era of caravels, spices and overseas conquest.

After its days as a gun-fort faded, its dank lower chambers became cells for political prisoners, while above, the same balconies once used to scan for incoming treasure ships now draw crowds gazing out over the wide tidal water.
puzzles.funFact: The rhinoceros carved into one of the tower's turrets around 1515 is thought to be the first depiction of the animal in European stone architecture; it commemorated a live rhino that King Manuel I had received as a gift and later shipped off to the Pope, only for the animal to drown in a storm en route.
puzzles.teaser: The last farewell of stone for sailors bound beyond the edge of the known world.

photo.description: a large tower sitting on top of a body of water

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast three-storey domed palace blazing with strings of golden light bulbs against a night sky, its pink-grey granite facade lined with arches, marble domes, and a tall central tower, set behind a wide ceremonial courtyard.
clues: On certain nights nearly 97,000 light bulbs are switched on at once, outlining every arch and dome of this royal residence so it glows like a single colossal lantern visible across the city.
After a wedding-day fire in 1897 gutted the old wooden royal home, a regent queen ruling on behalf of her teenage son commissioned a British architect to raise something grander in its place.
The building you see today was completed in 1912 in the Indo-Saracenic style, fusing Hindu, Mughal, Rajput and Gothic elements into one sprawling silhouette of domes and arches.
It is the ceremonial heart of a southern Indian state's most famous ten-day autumn festival, when this former princely capital becomes a stage for processions and torchlit pageantry.

On the festival's final day a 750-kilogram golden seat, plated in around 85 kilograms of gold, is hoisted onto a decorated tusker that carries a goddess's idol out of these gates toward the city's grounds.
puzzles.funFact: The palace's nightly illumination once used so many incandescent bulbs that it became one of southern India's signature spectacles - today around 97,000 bulbs light it up during the Dasara festival, switched on in unison for a golden glow seen for miles.
puzzles.teaser: When the festival lamps blaze, a golden seat and a goddess ride out through these gates.

photo.description: a large building with red domes with Mysore Palace in the background

puzzles.imageDescription: A slender, seven-arched sandstone footbridge threads between towering jagged rock pinnacles, suspended high above a deep forested gorge, with a hazy river valley stretching to the horizon under soft morning light.
clues: The very first landscape photographs ever taken in this country were shot from this dizzying perch in 1853, capturing a maze of stone needles that erosion carved over a million years.
A great Romantic painter immortalized these crags in his canvas of jagged spires looming above a river valley, helping turn a wild ravine into one of the continent's earliest tourist draws.
Crowds grew so large that the original timber walkway, thrown up by locals in the 1820s, was replaced in 1851 by an elegant span of pale local stone designed to blend into the cliffs.
Rising about 194 metres above a famous river southeast of Dresden, these pinnacles form the signature landmark of a national park whose nickname borrows from a neighbouring Alpine nation.
A graceful walkway of seven arches strides 76.5 metres across a gorge that plunges some 40 metres below, linking weathered towers of soft sandstone where climbers and hikers crowd the railings.
puzzles.funFact: The pale stone span you see today is the second bridge here: an earlier wooden walkway from 1824 was replaced in 1851 with sandstone precisely so it would blend into the surrounding cliffs.
puzzles.teaser: A stone thread stitched between sky-high stone needles, hanging over a hidden gorge.

photo.description: concrete bridge

puzzles.imageDescription: An immense, mile-deep chasm of horizontally banded red, ochre, and rust-colored rock layers receding in ridge after ridge to a hazy horizon, with a thin green river glinting far below at the bottom of the gorge.
clues: Its walls expose nearly two billion years of Earth's history in stacked layers of rock, and roughly five million people peer over its rim every year.
In 1869 a one-armed Civil War veteran, his right forearm lost at Shiloh, led the first known boat expedition blind into its rapids, not knowing whether a fatal waterfall waited downstream.
It was slowly cut over millions of years as a great river sliced downward while the surrounding plateau was pushed steadily upward, peeling back layer after layer of sediment.
It lies in the high desert of northern Arizona, carved into the Colorado Plateau by the river that gives the surrounding region its name.

From its forested South Rim you might spot a California condor riding the thermals; the giant scavengers were reintroduced here in 1996 after nearly going extinct, and they now nest in its painted cliffs.
puzzles.funFact: The dark Vishnu Schist at the canyon's base is nearly two billion years old, while the rim rock is comparatively young, leaving a roughly billion-year gap of missing rock layers that geologists call the 'Great Unconformity.'
puzzles.teaser: A mile straight down, two billion years of stone laid bare.

photo.description: brown rocky mountain under white clouds during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A slender silver ribbon of water free-falls nearly a kilometer down the sheer vertical cliff of a flat-topped, jungle-cloaked sandstone mesa, much of the stream dissolving into mist before it reaches the rainforest canopy below.
clues: At 979 meters, this is the tallest uninterrupted waterfall on the planet -- so high that much of its single 807-meter plunge scatters into mist long before reaching the ground.

It owes its common name to a daredevil American gold-prospecting aviator, who in 1937 crash-landed his small plane on the boggy summit above it and then spent eleven grueling days hiking back to civilization.

Long before any outsider arrived, the Indigenous Pemon people knew it as Kerepakupai Vena -- 'waterfall of the deepest place' -- pouring off one of the ancient flat-topped mountains they call the 'house of the gods.'
It tumbles off the rim of a sandstone tabletop mountain in the Gran Sabana of this South American nation's Bolivar State, inside a UNESCO-listed national park near the Orinoco watershed.
It so captivated a Pixar story team that they reimagined it as the dreamed-of 'Paradise Falls' -- the surreal cliff-top cascade toward which a balloon-borne house drifts in a 2009 animated film.
puzzles.funFact: The aviator it is named for, Jimmie Angel, first flew over it in 1933 while searching for a legendary gold ore bed; his plane sat stranded atop the mesa for 33 years until it was finally airlifted off in 1970 and restored.
puzzles.teaser: A ribbon of water that vanishes into mist before it ever touches the jungle floor.

photo.description: waterfalls in the middle of the forest

puzzles.seed: famous movie set you can visit
puzzles.imageDescription: A lush emerald hillside dotted with tiny round colorful doors set into grassy mounds, each with a low fence, a vegetable garden, and a crooked chimney; a great spreading tree crowns the highest hill above a thatched cottage, with a pond and an arched stone bridge below.
clues: This place holds a Guinness World Record as the largest purpose-built film set ever made, sprawling across roughly 14 acres of rolling green pasture that draws visitors from around the globe.
A famous director circling overhead in a small plane looked down and decided the unspoilt green hills below were like a slice of ancient England, perfect for a beloved fantasy world.

It began life as part of a 1,250-acre family sheep and beef farm; crews first built temporary facades here in 1999, then returned a decade later to construct everything permanently so fans could keep coming.
Tucked into the lush dairy-and-sheep country of this island nation's North Island, the warren of 44 little round doors sits in landscaped gardens you can tour any day of the week.

The great tree crowning the hill above the most famous little house is entirely fake: about 26 tonnes of fibreglass dressed with roughly 200,000 silk leaves imported from Taiwan, each wired on by hand and then repainted because the director disliked their shade.
puzzles.funFact: The 44 round doors were deliberately built in two different scales, with larger ones used to make full-sized actors look hobbit-small and smaller ones to make the taller Gandalf appear giant beside them.
puzzles.teaser: Forty-four little round doors, left standing on a green hill for the fans.

photo.description: green and brown tunnel surrounded by green trees during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A towering bell-shaped stupa sheathed entirely in gold leaf glows against a deep dusk sky, its tapering spire crowned with a jeweled umbrella that catches the light. At its base, a ring of countless tiny oil-lamp flames flickers as robed pilgrims circle the marble terrace beneath a bright full moon.
clues: Its crown alone is studded with more than five thousand diamonds, and the single gem at the very tip is said to weigh seventy-six carats — a fortune balanced where no visitor will ever reach.
Legend insists eight hairs given by the Buddha himself are enshrined within, making pilgrims believe the relics here outrank those of nearly any other shrine in the Buddhist world.

Earthquakes toppled earlier versions for centuries; a king rebuilt the present brick-and-gold form to roughly ninety-nine metres in the 1700s, then later rulers added the jeweled spire that crowns it today.
It rises on a low hill in this Southeast Asian nation's largest city, the former capital, where the dominant Theravada Buddhist faith shapes daily life.
Tonight, as the full moon ends the three-month rains retreat, the faithful ring its terraces with thousands of small oil lamps to light the Buddha's return from the heavens.
puzzles.funFact: Rather than being painted gold, the stupa is sheathed in real gold — an estimated 27 tonnes of gold plates and gold leaf — and by tradition devotees, including ordinary citizens, donate gold to keep its surface gleaming.
puzzles.teaser: Beneath a Lent-ending full moon, a mountain of gold answers ten thousand tiny flames.

photo.description: grey concrete temple during nighttime

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast ochre-brown structure of sun-dried earth rises above a dusty plain, its three tapering minarets crowned with ostrich-egg finials. Hundreds of pointed wooden stakes bristle from the smooth mud walls, casting sharp shadows in the Sahelian light, while a low market crowd gathers at its base.
clues: It is the single largest structure on Earth made entirely of sun-dried mud brick, rising on a raised platform that lifts it above the seasonal floods.

Each year the whole town turns out for a festive single-day labor: griots sing, neighborhoods race each other, and by nightfall the building wears a fresh coat of hand-smeared mud, with a small cash prize for the fastest team.

The version standing today was raised in 1907 under the master mason Ismaila Traore, atop the footprint of a far older sanctuary whose origins trace back centuries to a wealthy trans-Saharan trading town.

Set on the flood plain of the Bani River in the Sahel, this is the spiritual heart of a fabled inland-delta market town in West Africa, a place long linked by camel caravan to the gold and salt routes.
Bundles of palm wood, called toron, jut from the walls in neat rows; they are not mere decoration but a permanent, built-in scaffold that masons climb to renew the eroding earthen skin.
puzzles.funFact: The spiky wooden beams studding the walls, called toron, are not just decoration: they form a permanent built-in scaffold, so when the entire town replasters the building by hand in a single day each year, the ladders are already part of the architecture.
puzzles.teaser: A mountain of mud reborn by a thousand hands in a single day.

photo.description: white mosque

puzzles.imageDescription: Six colossal honey-colored Corinthian columns linked by a carved entablature soar against a blue sky on a stone terrace, the largest surviving fragment of a vast Roman sanctuary, with a smaller but near-complete temple and a green mountain valley visible behind.
clues: Lurking in a nearby quarry is the largest stone block ever carved by human hands — an unfinished monolith of roughly 1,650 tons, abandoned mid-cut and never moved.
Captivated 19th-century travelers and artists puzzled over how anyone could have lifted such impossible weights, and modern fringe writers still insist the work must have been done by giants or gods.
Founded over a god of the sun, the city was crowned 'Sun City' by Greek-speakers after Alexander, then rebuilt on a titanic scale as a Roman colony from the reign of the first emperor.
Set in a fertile high valley between two mountain ranges, this was Rome's grandest sanctuary in the eastern provinces — in a country on the Mediterranean's far-eastern shore.

In the great temple's foundation sit three dressed blocks each weighing some 800 tons, and of the 54 columns that once ringed it, just six still stand in a row — the tallest columns the classical world ever raised.
puzzles.funFact: The three enormous foundation stones known as the Trilithon each weigh around 800 tons — yet they were hoisted into a wall about seven meters off the ground, and to this day no one is certain exactly how the Romans did it.
puzzles.teaser: Six lonely giants stand guard over the heaviest stones men ever dared to move.

photo.description: a large stone structure with four pillars

puzzles.imageDescription: A graceful nine-span stone-and-brick viaduct curves through emerald jungle and tea-clad hills, its arches framing a misty gorge while a bright blue train inches across the top.
clues: This curved viaduct has no steel in its spans at all -- just stone block, brick and cement -- yet over a century later it still carries full passenger trains daily across a jungle gorge.
Locals nickname it 'the Bridge in the Sky,' because when you stand beneath it and look up, its row of openings frames nine separate patches of sky.

Work on it stalled when the steel shipment meant for the project was reportedly seized for World War I; rather than wait, local builders finished it around 1919-1921 entirely without metal in the arches.
It sits about 1,130 metres up in the misty tea-growing hill country of this island nation south of India, on the upcountry line between two small highland stations.
Around midday a bright blue express crawls across its curve while travellers crouch on the track for the perfect photo -- the signature shot of this teardrop island's railways.
puzzles.funFact: Because a wartime steel shortage halted the project, the arches were built from stone, brick and cement with no structural steel -- the only metal is in the rails and the pins holding them down.
puzzles.teaser: A blue train tiptoes across nine stone skies above the jungle.

photo.description: blue train on focus photography

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast walled palace courtyard of dark-tiled wooden pavilions with sweeping upturned eaves and red-and-green painted brackets, fronted by a towering triple-arched stone gate; jagged forested granite peaks rise directly behind the rooftops while modern city towers crowd the far horizon.
clues: With more than 56 million visitors logged since 2005, this is the single most-visited tourist site in its bustling capital city.
Its name, drawn from a line of an ancient Classic of Poetry verse, translates roughly to a place 'greatly blessed by heaven' with enduring prosperity.

Founded in 1395 as the very first and grandest of a new dynasty's palaces, it was burned to the ground during a 1590s invasion, then left in silent ruin for nearly 275 years before a powerful regent rebuilt it for his boy-king son in the 1860s.

It sits at the heart of a peninsular nation's capital, backed by a granite mountain and aligned on a grand ceremonial avenue, where guards in vivid blue, red and yellow court robes perform a costumed gate ceremony twice a day.

Pass beneath its three-arched main gate and you reach a wide stone-flagged court lined with rank markers, leading to the dynasty's largest throne hall where kings once issued edicts and received foreign envoys.
puzzles.funFact: The palace stood as a charred ruin for almost three centuries after being torched in 1592 — and it wasn't fully reconstructed until the 1860s, when the regent Heungseon Daewongun rebuilt some 330 buildings on the original site.
puzzles.teaser: Behind a towering gate, costumed sentries change watch where kings once ruled a dynasty.

photo.description: a tall building with a sky background

puzzles.imageDescription: A turreted medieval fortress of pale stone and red roofs clings to a craggy limestone bluff, its narrow towers rising sheer above a forested mountain pass; mist threads through the pines of the surrounding peaks, lending the silhouette a brooding, otherworldly air at dusk.
clues: Every autumn this clifftop keep throws a famous after-dark masquerade, drawing crowds who come to costume up and prowl its torchlit corridors until dawn -- a party built on a vampire who was pure invention.

A 19th-century Irish novelist who never set foot in this country borrowed its brooding image for the lair of his blood-drinking count -- yet the bloodthirsty 15th-century warlord nicknamed 'the Impaler' that the legend conflates with him only ever passed through the gorge below, never living here.
Saxon townsfolk raised the stone stronghold in 1377 under a charter from a Hungarian king, planting it to guard -- and tax -- the mountain pass between two old principalities.
It crowns a limestone bluff in the Southern Carpathians near Brasov, on the historic frontier between Transylvania and Wallachia.

In the 1920s a British-born queen made it her cherished retreat, hiring a Czech architect to soften the fortress with an English-style park, a tea house, and even a hydroelectric plant fed by mountain springs.
puzzles.funFact: The 15th-century warlord whose 'Impaler' nickname fuels the castle's vampire fame almost certainly never lived here -- and the novelist who made 'Dracula' a household word never visited the country at all, conjuring his Transylvania entirely from books read in London.
puzzles.teaser: On the night the veil thins, torchlight climbs a clifftop keep that fiction made immortal.

photo.description: a castle on top of a mountain with a cloudy sky

puzzles.imageDescription: A small, cone-shaped island rising steeply from a misty highland lake, its red-tiled village houses stacked up the slope and crowned by a colossal hollow statue of a standing man with one fist raised to the sky. At its shore, fishermen poise enormous round butterfly-shaped nets over still black water.
clues: This conical speck of land is crowned by a hollow statue nearly 50 metres tall -- visitors climb roughly 160 steps up through its body and into a raised fist, peering out at the lake through openings in the giant wrist.

The colossus honours an independence-hero priest of the early 1800s, and the spiral stairway inside is lined with murals telling his life story, painted over four years by a noted muralist of the 1930s.
The town's name means 'maize flower' in the local indigenous tongue, and its people descend from a pre-Hispanic civilisation that was never conquered by the Aztecs.
Set on a highland lake in the Mexican state of Michoacan, its fishermen are famous for lowering huge round 'butterfly' nets to catch a tiny endemic white fish.
On one autumn night, families paddle across black water with a single candle at each canoe's bow and keep an all-night, marigold-and-candle graveyard vigil for their dead.
puzzles.funFact: The crowning statue of independence hero Jose Maria Morelos rises about 47.75 metres -- edging out the Statue of Liberty's own figure (about 46 metres) -- and you can climb roughly 160 steps inside it, up through the body and into the raised fist, to a viewing window in the clenched hand.
puzzles.teaser: Cross the black water by candlelight to where a giant's raised fist watches over the marigold graves.

photo.description: green trees near city buildings under blue sky during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A maze of ochre-yellow, weathered wooden merchant houses lining narrow lanes along a slow river, strung overhead with hundreds of glowing silk lanterns in red, gold, and blue. A low covered footbridge with a tiled pagoda roof spans a side canal, and paper lanterns drift on the dark water.
clues: Once a month, on the night the moon is full, this riverside warren of streets cuts its electric lights so that the only glow comes from candle-lit silk lanterns and tiny paper boats floating on the water.

A community of foreign merchants here believed a giant subterranean monster's spine ran beneath their quarter, so they raised a small covered bridge-temple over the canal to pin it like a sword and calm the earthquakes back home.

From the 15th to the 19th century this was one of Southeast Asia's busiest trading ports, where Japanese, Chinese, Dutch and Persian ships exchanged silk, ceramics and spices, its roots reaching back to an earlier seafaring kingdom of Hindu temple-builders.
It sits on the banks of the Thu Bon River in the central coast's Quang Nam region, roughly 30 km south of a major port city, in a country shaped like a long S.
Today more than 400 tailor and silk shops crowd its lanes, stitching custom suits and dresses in a day or two—a living echo of the cloth trade that first made this little yellow-walled town rich.
puzzles.funFact: Each month on the 14th day of the lunar calendar, the town switches off its electric lighting for a Full Moon Lantern Festival, leaving the streets lit only by silk lanterns and candles floated on the river.
puzzles.teaser: A yellow-walled river port where, once a month, the lights go out and the lanterns take over.

photo.description: a group of people in small boats on a river

puzzles.imageDescription: A flamboyant Romantic-era palace of candy-bright crimson and canary-yellow towers, terracotta domes, and crenellated walls perched on a misty forested mountain peak, blending Moorish arches, Gothic spires and Manueline stone carving into a single fairy-tale silhouette above the treetops.
clues: Painted in dazzling red and yellow, this hilltop fantasy spent most of the 20th century weathered to a drab grey, until a 1990s restoration returned it to its original eye-popping colours, a change that initially scandalised conservative locals.

An art-loving king-consort, an immigrant prince who married the reigning queen, dreamed up the whole thing as a Romantic summer retreat, and personally designed a half-man, half-fish merman gateway as an allegory of the creation of the world.
It rose between the 1840s and 1850s atop the ruins of a 16th-century Hieronymite monastery that had stood on the peak since a chapel was raised there after a reported apparition of the Virgin Mary.

Crowning the second-highest crag of a forested coastal mountain range near the Atlantic, in this country's own Riviera region west of the national capital, it is the jewel of a UNESCO-listed cultural landscape.

A deliberate mash-up of Moorish onion domes, Gothic arches, Renaissance detail and the local sailor's-rope stonework of the Age of Discovery, it became one of the world's defining monuments of 19th-century Romanticism and one of this nation's seven officially chosen wonders.
puzzles.funFact: King Ferdinand II had the palace's vivid red and yellow walls painted on purpose, but the colours faded so completely over the 1900s that when they were restored to the original scheme in the 1990s, many Portuguese were shocked, having only ever known the building as grey.
puzzles.teaser: A king painted his daydream onto a mountaintop in colours the world later forgot.

photo.description: gray and yellow castle at the top of a hill

puzzles.imageDescription: A low grassy mound in flat northern farmland, completely engulfed by a dense thicket of wooden and metal crosses of every size, from towering carved timber beams to tiny rosaries draped in their thousands, narrow paths winding between them under an overcast Baltic sky.
clues: No one maintains it and no one is buried here, yet this modest mound now bristles with well over 100,000 crosses, rosaries and effigies left by anonymous pilgrims - and the count only keeps climbing.
In September 1993 a visiting Pope stood here and declared it a place of hope, peace, love and sacrifice, later sending a crucifix and urging Franciscan friars to build a monastery nearby.
The tradition is thought to have begun as mourning after a crushed 1831 uprising, when families with no bodies to bury planted crosses on an old hill fort to remember the dead and the disappeared.
It sits in flat farmland in the north of a small Baltic nation, a short drive from the city of Siauliai, near the road and rail line running toward Riga.

Three times an occupying regime sent bulldozers to flatten it, burning the wood and melting the metal for scrap - and three times locals crept back overnight to replant, turning a hill into an act of silent defiance.
puzzles.funFact: Soviet authorities bulldozed the site three times and even considered building a dam to flood it, but pilgrims kept sneaking back at night to replant crosses - and estimates today run well past 100,000, with some counts above 200,000.
puzzles.teaser: No one planted the first one, and no one can stop the rest.

photo.description: A bunch of crosses that are in the grass

puzzles.imageDescription: A steep, narrow high street of crooked Tudor and Georgian houses climbing toward a ruined Norman castle keep, set in a gap where a river cuts through chalk downland. By night the same streets fill with smoke, robed marchers bearing flaming crosses, and a river of torchlight.
clues: One night a year this small downland town of barely 17,000 people swells with crowds of up to 80,000, earning it the unofficial title 'bonfire capital of the world.'
Every year a 17th-century pontiff is rebuilt in effigy here only to be packed with fireworks and blown to pieces, while one society still marches behind a defiant 'No Popery' banner.
The fiery ritual born here mourns seventeen local Protestants burned at the stake between 1555 and 1557 under Mary I; today seventeen blazing crosses are carried through the streets in their memory.
It is the county town of East Sussex, sitting in a gap where a river slices through the chalk South Downs, guarded by a ruined Norman castle.

After flaming tar barrels are raced down the high street, one is hurled into the river below, re-enacting the night in 1847 when angry locals threatened to throw the magistrates in after the Riot Act was read.
puzzles.funFact: The town's commemoration is unusually pointed: it is the only place in Britain where bonfire societies still march under a 'No Popery' banner and ritually explode an effigy of Pope Paul V, the pope at the time of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot.
puzzles.teaser: Remember, remember -- the medieval town that turns into a river of fire.

photo.description: a lush green field with trees in the distance

puzzles.imageDescription: Two steep, jungle-cloaked volcanic spires rising abruptly out of brilliant turquoise Caribbean water, their pointed green summits framed by tropical haze and a curving palm-lined shoreline below.
clues: Two of these jungle-covered volcanic spires rise almost vertically straight out of the sea, the taller cresting around 798 meters, and they are so iconic to their island that their twin silhouette inspired the triangular emblem on the national flag.
A local artist designed that 1967 flag, its central triangular emblem meant to echo these peaks soaring sheer out of the water toward the sky as a symbol of the people's hope and aspirations.
These are hardened lava plugs, the eroded cores of ancient volcanoes, and the surrounding zone was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004 for both its beauty and its remarkable geology.
They flank a small Caribbean town on the island's southwest coast, near bubbling geothermal sulphur springs marketed as the world's only 'drive-in volcano.'
Climbers chug up the broader of the two cones through tropical forest in a few sweaty hours, while the slimmer, steeper neighbor is so sheer that guided ascents of it are tightly restricted.
puzzles.funFact: The two peaks are linked by a high ridge called Piton Mitan, and the wider one, Gros Piton, stands about 798 meters tall while its slimmer sibling Petit Piton reaches roughly 743 meters.
puzzles.teaser: Twin green daggers stabbing straight up from a turquoise sea.

photo.description: white yacht on body of water

puzzles.imageDescription: Steep limestone temple-pyramids with combed crests rise out of a dense green rainforest canopy under a hazy tropical sky, their grey stone tiers catching the light above an endless sea of treetops.
clues: Climb its tallest temple-pyramid and your eyes reach the top of the rainforest canopy from about 70 meters up, the height of a standing pre-Columbian tower that still pokes through the trees.
A filmmaker spotted it on a travel-agency poster in England, and the treetop view above the jungle became a far-off rebel moon in the first film of a galaxy far, far away.
Its rulers called their kingdom simply 'Mutul,' and a victorious lord raised that towering temple around AD 741 to crow over his conquests before the whole city was swallowed by forest and forgotten.
Buried in the Peten lowlands of this Central American nation, it was 'rediscovered' in 1848 by a local magistrate hacking through the trees, and its park became a World Heritage Site in 1979.
One king lies sealed in a funerary temple over the great plaza with offerings of jaguar pelts, jade, and rare spiny-oyster shells, a tomb found only in 1962 after centuries hidden inside the stone.
puzzles.funFact: The treetop view from atop its tallest pyramid stood in for the rebel base on the moon Yavin 4 in the original 1977 Star Wars film, after George Lucas reportedly saw the ruins on a travel poster in a London shop window.
puzzles.teaser: Stone giants pierce a sea of green where a galaxy far, far away once landed.

photo.description: a stone structure with trees and grass around it with Tikal in the background

puzzles.imageDescription: A towering five-storey facade of rose and salmon sandstone rises like a honeycomb against a clear sky, its hundreds of tiny arched lattice windows and domed crowns glowing warm above a busy bazaar street, with strings of festival lamps draped along its tiers.
clues: Its street-facing wall is pierced by 953 tiny latticed windows, a honeycomb screen designed so air would funnel through and keep the chambers cool without a single fan.
The king who commissioned it was a devout worshipper of the god Krishna, and the architect tiered the whole pyramidal facade so its silhouette would echo the deity's plumed crown.
Completed in 1799, it was raised as the public-facing screen of a royal women's quarters, a place from which to watch the world rather than to live in.
It edges the bustling bazaar of a Rajasthani capital nicknamed the 'Pink City' for the rose-washed buildings that share its sandstone hue.

Cloistered noblewomen, forbidden to be seen in public, would press against the cool lattices to watch the festival processions and lamp-lit Diwali parades flowing through the street below, unseen by the crowd.
puzzles.funFact: It is essentially a one-room-deep screen wall: many of the upper floors have no staircases at all, and the upper levels are reached only by gently winding ramps rather than steps.
puzzles.teaser: Behind 953 latticed eyes, hidden women watched the festival lamps below.

photo.description: brown concrete building during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A glassy, mirror-still ribbon of dark water threading between sheer ice-draped mountain walls that plunge straight into the sea, with stranded blue-white icebergs floating in the foreground under a pale polar sky.
clues: Barely 600 metres wide at its tightest squeeze yet hemmed by cliffs that soar over a kilometre overhead, this 11-km passage is so photogenic that early visitors burned through every roll of film they carried, earning it a nickname borrowed from a famous camera brand.

Oddly, this waterway honours a man who never came near the polar ice: it carries the name of a Belgian officer celebrated instead for his expeditions deep into the Congo River basin of central Africa.

First glimpsed by a German expedition in the 1870s, it was not actually sailed until December 1898, when a wooden Belgian ship became the first vessel to thread its narrows during a pioneering expedition that would later be trapped in winter pack ice.

It separates a small offshore island from a mountainous peninsula on the western flank of a long arm of land that points north toward South America, on the only continent with no permanent human population.

On calm days the water turns to a perfect mirror, so still that the surrounding peaks and floating bergs double exactly upon its surface, making this the climactic camera stop where nearly every ship full of red-jacketed travellers cuts its engines to drift in silence.
puzzles.funFact: The strait is named after Charles Lemaire, a Belgian explorer of the Congo who had no connection to Antarctica whatsoever; expedition leader Adrien de Gerlache simply chose to honour his compatriot when his ship first sailed through in 1898.
puzzles.teaser: A mirror of black water threading between walls of ice, where every camera comes out at once.

photo.description: a cruise ship with a mountain in the background

puzzles.imageDescription: A glowing orange lava lake churns inside a steep, dark crater at dusk, its molten surface cracking into glowing seams while plumes of sulfurous steam rise toward silhouetted hikers camped on the rim.
clues: This steep cone cradles what is widely called the largest lava lake on Earth -- a permanent pool of molten rock that adventurers camp beside on the crater rim to watch it boil through the night.

When its crater wall ruptured one morning in 1977, the entire lake drained in roughly half an hour, and the freakishly runny lava raced downhill at speeds estimated near 60 mph -- among the fastest flows ever witnessed -- overwhelming villages in minutes.

Its lava is so deadly because it is unusually poor in silica -- a silica-starved, alkali-rich melt that flows almost like water rather than the sluggish ooze of most volcanoes, a chemistry geologists tie to the deep rifting splitting the continent here.
Rising in the Virunga range along the Albertine Rift of eastern Africa, it looms barely a dozen kilometers above a lakeside city of roughly half a million people on the shore of Lake Kivu.

On a January night in 2002, glowing rivers from its flank poured straight through the heart of that nearby provincial capital, cutting the city in two, swallowing thousands of homes, and sending hundreds of thousands fleeing across the border on foot.
puzzles.funFact: Because its lava is so low in silica, the 1977 flows from this volcano sped downhill at up to about 100 km/h (60 mph) -- the fastest lava flows ever recorded, fast enough to outrun a fleeing person.
puzzles.teaser: A boiling orange cauldron that never sleeps, perched above a city that lives in its shadow.

photo.description: a body of water with a fire in it and mountains in the background

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast pale-stone triumphal arch straddling a road, its barrel-vaulted interior and walls densely inscribed with thousands of engraved names, crowned by a recumbent stone lion facing the open countryside beyond.
clues: Carved into its pale stone are the names of more than 54,000 soldiers who vanished without a grave, so many that the masons ran out of room and thousands more had to be listed elsewhere.
Every single evening since 1928, traffic through this archway is halted and buglers from the town's volunteer fire brigade step into the road to sound a solemn farewell call to the fallen.
A triumphal arch begun in the 1920s by a noted British architect, it was raised over the road by which troops once marched out toward the front, and unveiled in 1927 as a mausoleum to the missing.
It guards a road out of a small cloth-trading town in Flanders, in poppy country where a famous wartime poem was written; a stone lion rests on its roof, gazing east toward the old battlefields.

On the night this country was finally liberated in 1944, residents resumed the nightly bugle tribute beneath the arch even as fighting still echoed elsewhere in the town -- a vow kept unbroken ever since.
puzzles.funFact: The arch was designed to hold every name of the missing from the Ypres Salient, but it proved too small -- so an arbitrary cut-off of 15 August 1917 was set, and nearly 35,000 names of those who fell after that date were carved instead onto the curved memorial wall at nearby Tyne Cot.
puzzles.teaser: Every dusk the traffic stops, and a bugle remembers the names that have no graves.

photo.description: people walking on gray concrete building during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A steep cobbled lane climbs between dazzling whitewashed houses, every door, shutter, and window grille painted the same deep cobalt blue, with bougainvillea spilling over the walls and a hazy expanse of Mediterranean sea glittering far below the clifftop.
clues: Travel writers love to call this clifftop maze of white walls and cobalt doors the 'Santorini of North Africa' — though it was painting its houses long before anyone thought to compare it to a Greek isle.

In April 1914 three young modernist painters — among them an artist whose Tunisian fortnight is now seen as a turning point in 20th-century art — climbed this hill, settled onto the woven mats of its hilltop cafe overlooking the sea, and sketched it; the watercolour one of them made of that cafe became an enduring image of the place.
The village grew up around a 13th-century sanctuary built by a Sufi holy man on a hill once known as Jabal el-Menar, and wealthy families later filled it with breezy summer mansions.
It overlooks the gulf that the capital of this North African country is named for, just up the coast from the ruins of an ancient Phoenician rival of Rome.

In 1915 a colonial-era decree fixed its look forever — owners must keep walls limewashed white and woodwork a single shade of blue — and you can still sip mint tea sprinkled with pine nuts on the woven mats of a famous terraced cafe above the water.
puzzles.funFact: When painters Paul Klee, August Macke, and Louis Moilliet passed through Tunisia in April 1914, the trip proved so transformative that it is now regarded as a key art-historical event of the 20th century — and August Macke's watercolour of the village's hilltop Cafe des Nattes remains one of its most famous images.
puzzles.teaser: Cobalt doors, lime-white walls, and a sea that never stops being blue.

photo.description: white concrete building near body of water during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A surreal, sun-baked landscape of giant rounded granite boulders scattered across an open plain, dotted with weathered stone temple towers and pillared pavilions. At its heart stands an intricately carved stone chariot, its wheels and tiered shrine cut entirely from rock, framed by an empty, dusty courtyard.
clues: A carved stone chariot here is so iconic that a national government printed it on a banknote still in circulation, putting a piece of this ruin into millions of wallets.
A visiting Portuguese horse-trader marvelled that merchants in its market streets piled up rubies, diamonds and pearls beside the everyday cloth, as if precious stones were just another commodity.

It rose as the capital of a powerful 14th-century empire, then thrived for two centuries before a single catastrophic defeat in 1565 saw the victors loot and burn it over months, after which it was simply abandoned.
Set among gravity-defying boulder hills on the southern bank of a river in east-central Karnataka, locals long identified these very rocks with a mythical monkey kingdom from an ancient epic.

Wander its open-air bazaar today and you can still trace the long colonnaded stalls where horses and gems once changed hands, all clustered around a Shiva temple whose tower has welcomed pilgrims continuously for centuries.
puzzles.funFact: At its height the city's bazaars reportedly traded diamonds so openly that gems were measured out by weight in heaps; the stone chariot that symbolizes the site today appears on India's 50-rupee note.
puzzles.teaser: A field of giant boulders cradles the stone heart of a vanished, diamond-rich empire.

photo.description: brown concrete building during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A colossal gleaming silver warrior on horseback rises 40 meters from a flat, empty grassland under a vast pale sky, perched atop a circular columned base. The mirror-bright stainless-steel rider grips reins and gazes toward the horizon, dwarfing tiny visitors gathered at its feet.
clues: At 40 metres of mirror-bright steel, it ranks as the tallest equestrian statue on Earth, sheathed in roughly 250 tonnes of stainless steel that flares blinding silver across an empty grassland.
Legend says a young warrior, riding home in 1177 from a meeting with an ally, found a golden whip on this very spot -- an omen of fortune that the monument was raised to mark.
Unveiled in 2008, it was built to crown the 800th anniversary of the empire its rider founded, set atop a round hall ringed by 36 columns for the 36 rulers of his dynastic line.
It stands on the open steppe of central Asia, about 54 km east of this landlocked nation's capital, near a river where nomadic herders still graze their horses.
Visitors climb up through the chest and neck of the horse to an observation deck on its head -- where, deliberately, the giant rider stares east toward the land said to be his birthplace.
puzzles.funFact: The horse alone is hollow enough to house a lift and stairway: tourists ride and climb up through the animal's neck to emerge on the top of its head, level with the rider's chest, for a panoramic view of the steppe.
puzzles.teaser: A silver horseman blazes alone on an endless sea of grass.

photo.description: man riding horse statue under cloudy sky during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A rugged, sun-bleached savanna island rising from turquoise water, its golden hills dotted with lontar palms, and a curving beach where white sand blushes a soft rose-pink. A massive, armored lizard with a forked tongue patrols the dry grassland in the foreground.
clues: This is the only place on Earth where you can meet, in the wild, the planet's largest living lizard - a reptile that can top three meters and weigh over 160 kilograms.
In 2006 a female of this island's signature reptile, kept far away in an English zoo, stunned scientists by laying eggs that hatched with no male involved at all - a true virgin birth.

Western science only learned of the giant 'land crocodiles' here after rumors reached a Dutch officer in 1910; a museum director published the first formal description in 1912, and the surrounding park became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991.
It sits in the Lesser Sunda chain of this Southeast Asian archipelago nation, between two larger islands, ringed by reefs and savanna rather than rainforest.
Among its dry hills hides a beach that glows a soft rose, its sand tinted pink by crushed fragments of red coral - one of only a handful of such shores anywhere in the world.
puzzles.funFact: The island's namesake dragons have a venomous bite: their venom contains toxins that prevent blood from clotting, so prey that escapes the initial attack can bleed out and go into shock.
puzzles.teaser: Where rose-pink sand meets the last wild dragons.

photo.description: brown mountain beside body of water during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast half-elliptical plaza enclosed by a curved brick-and-tile building with two tall towers at its ends, fronted by a 500-meter canal crossed by four ornate balustraded bridges. Rowboats drift on the water past a sweeping sequence of colorful azulejo-tiled alcoves set into the facade.
clues: This sweeping semicircular square is wrapped by a roughly 500-meter canal where visitors still paddle small rowboats, earning it the nickname of a southern 'Venice'.
In a galaxy far, far away it stood in as the royal city of a watery planet: Anakin and Padme stroll across its bridges in a 2002 blockbuster, the plaza standing in for an alien capital.
It was raised in the late 1920s as the grand centerpiece of a world's fair celebrating ties between the host nation and the Americas, blending Baroque, Renaissance and Moorish-revival design.
Set within a sprawling park in the largest city of Andalusia, in southern Spain, its facade carries 48 tiled alcoves, one for each province of the country.
Four bridges spanning its moat each stand for an old kingdom of the realm, while couples pose at the ceramic bench of their own home province along the painted curve.
puzzles.funFact: Each of the 48 tiled alcoves lining the plaza is dedicated to a different Spanish province in alphabetical order, and visitors traditionally seek out and photograph the bench matching their own home province.
puzzles.teaser: A tiled crescent where rowboats glide and a galaxy far, far away once landed.

photo.description: a couple of people riding on the back of a horse drawn carriage

puzzles.imageDescription: A gleaming snow-white neoclassical cathedral crowned by a tall green central dome flanked by four smaller green domes, rising above a vast cobblestone square at the top of a sweeping 60-metre-wide grand staircase, with zinc statues of apostles silhouetted along the rooflines.
clues: Roughly half a million visitors a year climb toward this dazzling white temple, whose green-domed silhouette has become the unofficial postcard image of an entire Nordic capital.
Tradition holds that it was a visiting emperor who suggested adding the monumental sweeping staircase that now lets crowds spill down into the square below for festivals and graduations.
Begun in 1830 and not finished until 1852, it was raised as a tribute to a Russian tsar who ruled the land at the time and was originally dedicated to a saint who shared his name.
It stands at the climax of a Greek-cross plan atop a grand square in a Lutheran Nordic country that spent a century under Russian rule before winning independence in 1917.

Look up and twelve larger-than-life zinc apostles watch over the rooflines, forming one of the world's biggest single gatherings of zinc statuary, cast in Berlin before being hoisted into place in 1849.
puzzles.funFact: Although it looks like a centuries-old monument, the cathedral's famous four small green corner domes weren't part of the original design at all; they were added by Engel's successor Ernst Lohrmann to echo the great Russian cathedrals of St Petersburg.
puzzles.teaser: White as snow, green-domed, and reigning over a grand square at the top of a hundred steps.

photo.description: white concrete mosque near body of water

puzzles.imageDescription: A colossal stepped pyramid of dark volcanic stone rises against a hazy highland sky, anchoring a vast grid of ruined platforms. A wide, dead-straight ceremonial avenue runs for kilometers between flanking temple bases, dotted with tiny visitors who give a sense of the monument's staggering scale.
clues: At its height around 1,500 years ago this was the largest city in all of the Americas, sprawling across some 20 square kilometers and home to well over 100,000 people -- bigger than most European cities of its day.

The much later empire that dominated this region revered the ruins as sacred ground, believing this was the very place where the gods sacrificed themselves to set the sun and moon in motion -- so they gave it a name meaning roughly 'the place where the gods were created.'

Its true builders left no readable writing, so their own name and language remain unknown; the metropolis flourished for centuries before being burned and abandoned around the 7th century, leaving only later visitors to invent the names we use today.

Set in a highland valley about 40 km northeast of this nation's capital, the complex is famous for a colossal stepped pyramid -- one of the largest in the world by volume -- and a broad, arrow-straight processional avenue that the region's later people grimly nicknamed for the dead.

In 2014 archaeologists crawling a sealed tunnel beneath the feathered-serpent temple found pools of shimmering liquid mercury and walls glittering with pyrite, perhaps meant to mimic an underworld river leading toward a still-undiscovered royal tomb.
puzzles.funFact: The famous Pyramid of the Sun and Avenue of the Dead are not the names its builders used -- those titles were coined centuries later by the Aztecs, who stumbled on the already-ruined metropolis and assumed gods, not people, had raised it.
puzzles.teaser: A city so old that even an empire of conquerors found only silent ruins and called it the birthplace of the gods.

photo.description: a group of people standing in front of a pyramid

puzzles.imageDescription: A clear, fast-flowing river cascading over ancient rock, its bed carpeted in vivid scarlet and magenta aquatic plants streaked with patches of yellow and green, set against lush tropical highlands and rounded quartzite outcrops.
clues: For only a few weeks each year, from roughly late July through November, this waterway's bed blazes red, yellow, green and black, earning it the nickname the River of Five Colors.
Locals long called it 'the river that ran away from paradise,' and for decades it was a place few outsiders could even reach, let alone admire.
The dazzling crimson is no mineral or pollution: it comes from an endemic aquatic plant that clings to the rocks and turns brilliant red only when sunlight and water levels are just right.

It threads through ancient quartzite outcrops over a billion years old on the western edge of the Guiana Shield, in a remote national park of this South American country, eventually feeding a tributary of the Orinoco basin.

Off-limits to visitors for roughly two decades because armed guerrillas controlled the surrounding wilderness, it reopened to tourists in 2009, who now fly in to a tiny frontier town to glimpse the brief 'liquid rainbow.'
puzzles.funFact: The river's famous red color is produced by a single endemic plant, Macarenia clavigera, which only blooms its vivid scarlet when the water level and sunlight reach a narrow seasonal sweet spot, too deep and the current blocks the sun, too shallow and the plant dries out.
puzzles.teaser: For a few magical weeks a year, a riverbed bursts into a flowing rainbow.

photo.description: clear crystal

puzzles.imageDescription: A cluster of jagged golden-limestone sea stacks rising abruptly from churning turquoise and white surf beneath sheer ochre cliffs, viewed from a clifftop boardwalk under a vast Southern Ocean sky.
clues: Despite a name promising a round dozen, this cluster of offshore towers never actually had that many, and the count keeps shrinking as they topple into the sea one by one.
An English sailor first dubbed the formation the 'Sow and Piglets,' picturing a mother pig and her young among the rocks before a far grander, more reverent name took hold.
In 1922 tourism promoters rebranded the humble pig-and-piglets nickname into something biblical and majestic, purely to lure more visitors to this remote stretch of coast.
They stand just off a celebrated scenic driving route in the state of Victoria, where the Southern Ocean hammers soft yellow limestone bluffs in a national park.
At 9:18 on a winter morning in July 2005, a 50-metre tower crumbled into the waves in front of stunned onlookers, dropping the standing count yet again.
puzzles.funFact: The formation was never home to twelve stacks despite the name; there were only ever nine, and after collapses in 2005 and 2009, just seven remain standing today.
puzzles.teaser: Apostles in name only, vanishing tower by tower into a restless southern sea.

photo.description: rock formation on seashore

puzzles.imageDescription: A vast, glassy expanse of turquoise water meeting a hazy horizon, fringed by golden sand beaches and rounded granite boulders, with brightly colored small fish darting through clear shallows and a wooden dugout canoe drawn up on the shore.
clues: This single body of water holds more fish species than any other lake on the planet, including hundreds of jewel-toned cichlids found nowhere else.
A famous Victorian missionary-explorer reached its shores in 1859 and, watching fishermen's lanterns shimmer across the dark surface, gave it a poetic nickname that stuck: the 'Lake of Stars'.
In 1984 a slice of its southern waters became the world's first freshwater national park, later listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its Galapagos-like explosion of fish evolution.
It forms most of the eastern border of the small landlocked country it is named for, in the southern reaches of the East African Rift, also touching Mozambique and Tanzania.
Snorkelers here chase clouds of small, brilliantly striped rocky-shore fish that locals call 'mbuna', and at night the dark water glitters with the lamps of dugout fishermen.
puzzles.funFact: Its cichlid fish are so spectacularly diverse that scientists compare them to Darwin's Galapagos finches: hundreds of distinct species evolved here, with some estimates exceeding 1,000, the vast majority found in this lake alone.
puzzles.teaser: A turquoise inland sea where fishermen's lanterns mirror the night sky.

photo.description: a small boat floating on top of a river next to a lush green hillside

puzzles.imageDescription: The interior of a 19th-century Persian prayer hall at dawn, where low morning sun streams through tall multicolored stained-glass windows and scatters a kaleidoscope of red, blue, yellow, and green light across spiraled stone columns and patterned Persian carpets on the floor.
clues: For a few fleeting minutes after sunrise, this prayer hall becomes one of the most photographed interiors on Earth, as worshippers and visitors are bathed head to toe in a kaleidoscope of colored light.

Its patron earned his lordly honorific almost by accident: after a chance roadside encounter with the reigning shah in the northern province of Mazandaran, he was granted the very title that this building now carries.

Built over roughly a dozen years and finished in 1888 during the dynasty that ruled before the modern era, it was the work of a master architect who had already designed a celebrated royal garden in the same city.
It rises in a rose-tiled southern Persian city famous for poets, nightingales, and gardens, tucked into an old quarter not far from a glittering mirror-walled pilgrimage shrine.

Its winter hall is screened by carved wooden doors set with panes of red, azure, yellow, orange, and green glass, deliberately oriented so the dawn light, and not the midday sun, performs the daily miracle of color on the carpets.
puzzles.funFact: Despite its worldwide fame as a temple of light, the rainbow effect lasts only a short window in the early morning; by afternoon the colored glow fades, so photographers line up before sunrise to catch it.
puzzles.teaser: At first light, the carpets catch fire with rainbows.

photo.description: a large room with stained glass windows in it

puzzles.imageDescription: An endless labyrinth of tidal channels winds through dense, low green mangrove canopy under a hazy delta sky, the muddy brackish water mirroring the tangled prop roots at the forest's edge.
clues: Spanning over 10,000 square kilometers, this is the single largest mangrove forest on Earth, a tidal wilderness so vast it forms a shifting maze of islands and saltwater channels.

Forest dwellers here pray to a guardian goddess revered by both Hindus and Muslims before entering the trees; she is believed to shield honey-gatherers and woodcutters from a demon who takes the form of a man-eating big cat.
The place takes its name from a salt-tolerant mangrove tree native to its swamps, a hardwood species that thrives where freshwater rivers meet the brackish sea.
It sprawls across the lower delta where the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers empty into the Bay of Bengal, straddling the border of two South Asian nations.
It is the only mangrove on the planet whose tigers have learned to swim between islands and hunt in the water, and in this forest those tigers are the leading cause of human death.
puzzles.funFact: The tigers here are such strong swimmers and so prone to attacking people that fishermen and honey-collectors have worn face masks on the backs of their heads, exploiting the cats' reluctance to attack a person who appears to be facing them.
puzzles.teaser: Where the tide breathes through the trees and the apex predator can swim.

photo.description: lake surrounded with tall green trees

puzzles.imageDescription: A colossal seated stone Buddha, roughly the height of a 20-story building, carved directly into a reddish sandstone river cliff. Tiny tourists cluster around the enormous bare feet at the water's edge, while the serene face gazes out over the muddy confluence of three rivers far below.
clues: At 71 metres, this is the tallest pre-modern statue on Earth and the largest stone Buddha ever carved -- its ears alone are 7 metres long and a single toenail is big enough for a person to sit on.
The whole thing was the life's work of a devout monk who, legend says, gouged out his own eyes to prove his sincerity to corrupt officials trying to seize the construction funds.

Carving began in 713 during the Tang dynasty after the monk saw boats wrecked in the deadly rapids below, and the rubble was dumped into the river to calm the currents; it took roughly 90 years and three generations to finish.
It sits at the violent confluence of three rivers in southern Sichuan province, China, where a representation of the future Buddha was set to watch over the water and protect the boatmen.

Hidden inside the figure is an ingenious drainage system woven into the 1,021 coiled curls of its hair and behind its ears, secretly carrying away rainwater so the stone has resisted erosion for 1,200 years.
puzzles.funFact: A clever drainage network is concealed in the statue's 1,021 spiral hair coils, behind its ears and in its chest -- this hidden plumbing has quietly drawn off rainwater and kept the figure from eroding for over a thousand years.
puzzles.teaser: A mountain-sized monk's gift, gazing forever at the river it was built to tame.

photo.description: brown concrete statue near green trees during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A square moated old town glowing at night, its grid of more than three dozen ancient golden-spired temples lit up while thousands of paper sky lanterns drift upward over the rooftops and small candlelit floats glide along a nearby river beneath a mist-wrapped mountain.
clues: More than 300 Buddhist temples crowd this northern valley city, with around 40 of them packed inside a single square mile ringed by an ancient water-filled moat.

On the twelfth-month full moon, locals here release thousands of glowing khom loi sky lanterns at once -- the dreamlike floating-light scene many travelers compare to a famous animated 'lost princess' film.
A king moved his capital here in 1296 after his earlier riverside settlement kept flooding, laying out a perfectly square walled grid with five gates and a wide encircling moat.
Nicknamed the 'Rose of the North,' it was the proud capital of the Lan Na kingdom, sits on the Ping River, and is watched over by a sacred temple-topped mountain to its west.
Its very name simply means 'new city,' and during the festival its people send wishes skyward on lanterns while floating candlelit krathongs down the river to ask the water goddess for forgiveness.
puzzles.funFact: The city's grid is laid out as a near-perfect square moat about 1.6 km on each side, dug by a reported workforce of 40,000 men who finished most of the walls, gates and moat in roughly four months back in the 1290s.
puzzles.teaser: A thousand wishes rise on paper flames over an 800-year-old moated city of golden spires.

photo.description: brown and white concrete house surrounded by green trees during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A weathered grey granite boulder sits in a sandy pit at the bottom of a stone enclosure, the year "1620" chiseled into its face. A neoclassical columned canopy of pale granite shelters it from above, and beyond the railing a harbor and waterfront stretch toward the sea.
clues: Far smaller than its legend, this celebrated stone has shrunk to roughly a third of its original size, much of it carried off in pieces by souvenir hunters over the centuries.
In 1774, when townsfolk tried to haul it away, it split clean in two along a crack -- and revolutionaries seized on the omen as a sign the colonies were about to break from the Crown.

No early settler ever wrote a word about it; its fame rests on an aged church elder who, in 1741, was carried to the water's edge to point it out as the very spot where travelers from across the sea first stepped ashore in 1620.
On a harbor in Massachusetts, it sits at the heart of a small waterfront park honoring the people whose arrival is now marked by an autumn feast of thanks.
Look closely and you will see a single date carved into its grey face -- a number added only in 1880 -- as it rests in a shallow pit beneath a columned canopy of granite, just steps from the tide.
puzzles.funFact: The famous "1620" was not carved by the people who landed -- it was chiseled into the rock in 1880, and earlier estimates suggest the original boulder may have weighed as much as ten times what survives today.
puzzles.teaser: A nation's harvest feast traces back to one shrinking grey boulder by the tide.

photo.description: a large sailboat docked at a pier

puzzles.imageDescription: An endless sea of more than a thousand near-identical conical green hills rolling to the horizon under a tropical sky, their grassy domes uniform in size and spacing like giant scattered mounds across a wide island plain.
clues: Spread across roughly fifty square kilometers, more than a thousand near-identical dome-shaped mounds rise from a single island plain, and in the dry months their grass cover browns until the whole field looks dusted in cocoa.

Local legend gives two versions: in one, two warring giants hurled boulders and sand at each other for days; in another, a lovestruck giant named Arogo wept so hard over the death of a mortal woman that his fallen tears hardened into these countless hills.

Their true origin is geological, not mythical: marine limestone laid down in a shallow sea was thrust upward by colliding tectonic plates, then sculpted by rain and groundwater into hundreds of remarkably uniform conical karst mounds.
Scattered through the towns of Carmen, Batuan, and Sagbayan on an island in the central Visayas, this formation is so beloved it appears on the local provincial flag and seal.

An American geologist counted 1,268 of the mounds here back in 1924; today they are honored as this nation's third declared National Geological Monument, with a hilltop viewing deck drawing visitors to gaze over the seemingly endless ranks of green cones.
puzzles.funFact: In 1924, American geologist Warren D. Smith tallied 1,268 of the symmetrical mounds, but later surveys count as many as 1,776 of them spread across the island.
puzzles.teaser: A thousand grassy domes that brown like cocoa, born (so they say) from a giant's tears.

photo.description: a group of large mounds in the middle of a forest

puzzles.imageDescription: A broad reverse-S waterway curving between rows of weathered pastel palazzi with arched windows and striped mooring poles; slim black boats with curved prows glide past, and a single grand stone bridge arches over the water in the haze.
clues: This roughly 3.8-kilometer waterway is the main thoroughfare of a city that has no cars at all -- residents and visitors commute by boat, and over 170 palaces from the 13th to 18th centuries line its banks.

Each September, costumed crews row replicas of ancient ceremonial vessels down this water in a regatta first held in the 13th century, a pageant that revives the maritime glory of a republic that once ruled the seas.

The waterway is believed to follow the former bed of a river that once emptied into the surrounding lagoon, and the whole city above it stands on millions of wooden piles driven into the soft mud, preserved for centuries by the oxygen-starved water.
It threads through a lagoon city in northeastern Italy, and for centuries a single arched stone bridge was the ONLY foot crossing between its two banks until a second was finally added in the 1850s.

Slender black boats with curved metal prows, each handled by a single standing oarsman, ferry passengers past front doors that open straight onto the water -- a craft so tied to this place that they are weighed and measured by an official guild.
puzzles.funFact: The wooden piles beneath the city have survived more than a thousand years because they sit in oxygen-poor lagoon mud, where the lack of air stops the fungi that would otherwise rot the timber -- effectively petrifying it into a stone-hard foundation.
puzzles.teaser: Where the streets are made of water and the front doors open onto the tide.

photo.description: Venice, Italy during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A cluster of pastel medieval merchant houses and cobbled lanes opening onto a town hall square, dominated by an ornate red-brick, stepped-gable guild house whose Gothic facade is studded with gilded statues and an astronomical clock, with a tall slender church spire rising behind the rooftops.
clues: A marble plaque set into this capital's town hall square cobbles claims, in eight languages, that the world's first decorated public Christmas tree was raised here in 1510 - a boast a rival Baltic city next door hotly disputes.

The cobbled square at its heart is guarded by a granite statue of a legendary paladin - the sword-bearing knight of Charlemagne immortalised in a famous medieval epic poem - and the tip of his upright blade marks the zero point from which distances to other European capitals are still measured; local lore holds that as long as that sword stays sharp, the city will remain free.

Born as a fortified river-mouth trading post in 1201, the place grew rich after 1282 as one of the easternmost anchors of the Hanseatic League, its warehouses linking the interior of the continent to Baltic and North Sea shipping lanes.

Strung along the lower Daugava in the Baltic states, its huddle of gabled houses and a slim church spire climbing roughly 123 metres earned the whole quarter a UNESCO listing in 1997, partly for holding what is called Europe's finest concentration of Art Nouveau just beyond its medieval core.

The ornate guild hall at its heart, crowned by a 1626 astronomical clock, was blasted to rubble on 29 June 1941, dynamited by Soviet authorities in 1948, and only resurrected from old drawings between 1996 and 2000 to mark the city's 800th birthday.
puzzles.funFact: The Brotherhood of the Blackheads were unmarried merchants, and once a member married he had to leave the guild - so their grand banqueting house effectively doubled as a clubhouse for the city's eligible bachelor traders.
puzzles.teaser: Where bachelor sailor-merchants once toasted an African saint beneath gilded gables on a Baltic river.

photo.description: an aerial view of a city with a river in the background

puzzles.imageDescription: A slender, tapering concrete spire soars above a glass-and-steel downtown skyline beside a vast lake, its bulging upper observation pod and needle-thin antenna mast catching the light against a clear sky.
clues: For 32 years it reigned as the world's tallest free-standing structure, a title it only surrendered in 2007 when a glittering desert skyscraper finally rose higher.

Thrill-seekers now buckle into a harness and stroll hands-free around a narrow ledge near the top, an exposed urban walk that Guinness World Records certified as the highest of its kind on any building.
It was dreamed up by a national railway company in the early 1970s, partly to fix the city's broadcast signals and partly to flaunt the strength and ambition of the country's industry.
Rising beside one of the Great Lakes, this concrete needle defines the skyline of the largest city in its country, the commercial heart of a vast northern, officially bilingual nation.

Lightning hits its slender shaft roughly 75 times a year, drained harmlessly to the ground by copper strips, while diners revolve slowly in a restaurant suspended hundreds of metres over the waterfront.
puzzles.funFact: When it opened in 1976, its glass-floor and revolving restaurant sat so high that staff had to be trained for the building's gentle sway, which can move the top of the antenna by more than a metre in high winds.
puzzles.teaser: A concrete needle that ruled the skies for a generation, where the brave now walk the rim with nothing but a tether.

photo.description: photo of high-rise buildings near body of calm water during daytime

puzzles.imageDescription: A near-perfect green cone rises sharply above a blanket of tropical rainforest, its summit often wreathed in cloud. At its foot, a vast turquoise reservoir stretches across the lowlands, with steaming hot springs and lush jungle framing the symmetrical peak.
clues: For 42 years this near-perfect cone was the most active volcano in its country, and at night the red glow of lava trickling down its flanks could be seen from the town below, until the show finally went quiet in 2010.

It became the unofficial emblem of a small nation's entire eco-tourism boom; travelers came not just to see it but to soak in the geothermal hot springs that bubble up at its base, heated by the molten rock within.
Cloaked in dense vegetation, it was thought to be a harmless, long-extinct hill, dormant for centuries, until one morning in 1968 it suddenly exploded, burying three villages and killing 87 people.
This stratovolcano stands in the northern lowlands of a Central American country famous for its biodiversity, rising straight out of the rainforest in the province of Alajuela.
Spreading at its foot is the country's largest lake, an artificial reservoir enlarged by a 1970s hydroelectric dam that drowned two old towns whose residents had to be resettled.
puzzles.funFact: After centuries of apparent dormancy, the volcano roared back to life on the morning of July 29, 1968, and the artificial lake at its base, now the country's largest, was created by a dam that submerged two entire towns whose residents were relocated.
puzzles.teaser: A jungle cone that slept for centuries, then lit up the night sky.

puzzles.imageDescription: Towering streaked walls of white, gray, and black marble plunge nearly vertically into a narrow chasm, where a glacial-turquoise river churns far below. A ribbon of road and dark tunnel mouths are carved directly into the polished stone cliffs, and mist drifts between the soaring canyon faces.
clues: It is celebrated as one of only three river-cut gorges on Earth carved entirely through solid marble, sharing that rarity with canyons in India and Bulgaria.
A small cliff-clinging shrine here perpetually weeps over a waterfall, built to honor the 226 men who lost their lives blasting a single mountain road through the rock.
Beginning in 1956, demobilized soldiers spent four years hammering and dynamiting a highway by hand through walls of pure stone, opening the route to traffic in 1960.
On the rugged east coast of this island nation, near the city of Hualien, a turquoise river called the Liwu has sliced this chasm more than 1,000 meters deep into the mountains.
Walk the narrowest stretch and you pass through a tunnel pocked with holes the swirling river drilled into the cliff, while platforms reveal the road corkscrewing through nine sharp turns far below.
puzzles.funFact: The gorge is one of only three river-carved canyons in the world cut entirely through pure marble, and the cliffside Eternal Spring Shrine was built to honor the 226 veterans who died blasting the Central Cross-Island Highway through the stone by hand.
puzzles.teaser: A turquoise river and a road carved by hand through a mountain of marble.

puzzles.imageDescription: A snorkeler drifts through sunlit emerald water densely filled with thousands of translucent, amber-gold pulsing creatures, jungle-covered limestone walls rising steeply around the enclosed basin under a tropical sky.
clues: Millions of soft, harmless creatures here perform a daily commute, swimming clear across this enclosed body of water and back again, all to chase the moving sunlight.
Cut off from the open sea for roughly 12,000 years, the inhabitants evolved in such total isolation that they lost almost all of their ability to sting, making them safe for swimmers to glide among.

It was carved when the last ice age ended: rising seas flooded a limestone basin, and when the water settled, a population of marine animals was sealed inside, connected to the ocean only by tiny fissures too narrow to escape through.
Reached by speedboat through a turquoise maze of mushroom-shaped jungle islets in the western Pacific nation of Palau, part of a lagoon inscribed by UNESCO in 2012.

Beneath about 15 meters the water turns into a lifeless, oxygen-free zone laced with poisonous gas; the golden swarm at the surface stays in the sunlit shallows, also dodging the shaded shores where their only predators, the anemones, wait.
puzzles.funFact: The lake's endemic golden jellyfish subspecies is named etpisoni after a former Palauan president, and the animals farm symbiotic algae in their tissues, rotating through the sunlight each day so the algae can photosynthesize and feed them in return.
puzzles.teaser: Drift through a living golden cloud that chases the sun across a hidden lake.
