puzzles.imageDescription: An endless hall of slender jasper and marble columns supporting a hypnotic forest of double-tiered arches striped in alternating red brick and white stone, vanishing into shadow under a low ceiling pierced by warm shafts of light.
clues: Beneath one roof here stand roughly 850 columns of jasper, marble, granite and onyx, forming a 'petrified forest' so vast it was once among the largest prayer halls on Earth.

An emperor who authorized a drastic alteration to this hall is said to have lamented afterward: 'You have built what could be built anywhere, but you have destroyed something that was unique in the world.'
It was begun in 785-786 by an exiled emir who, tradition holds, raised it over the divided remains of a Visigothic Christian church on the same ground.
Its hypnotic double arches, striped in red brick and white stone, rise in this Andalusian city on the Guadalquivir, long the dazzling capital of Moorish Iberia.

After Christian knights took the city in 1236, worshippers kept the arcades intact for centuries, then carved a full Renaissance cathedral nave straight into the middle of the prayer hall, leaving two religions layered under a single roof.
puzzles.funFact: Unlike a church converted to a mosque, this building went the other way and then kept both: in the 16th century a complete Christian cathedral was constructed inside the existing Muslim prayer hall, so the choir and high altar sit surrounded on all sides by the original Islamic arches.
puzzles.teaser: Two faiths, one roof, and a forest of candy-striped arches that never seems to end.

puzzles.imageDescription: A dense huddle of baroque domes, copper-green spires and pastel facades crowded along a swift green river, all watched over by a vast pale-stone fortress perched on a wooded crag above the rooftops, with snow-dusted Alpine foothills closing in behind.
clues: The fortress crowning this town is the largest fully preserved castle in Central Europe, never once taken by foreign troops in over 900 years, and still draws close to a million visitors a year.

On St Nicholas Eve each December, hundreds of fur-clad, horned demons brandishing birch switches are loosed through its baroque lanes -- the local incarnation of a folkloric punisher who shadows the saint handing out sweets.

The town owes both its name and its fortune to 'white gold': the mineral hauled from nearby mountain mines funded the palaces and cathedrals that earned it the nickname 'Rome of the North,' built by Italy-inspired prince-archbishops.

Set on a fast green river at the northern foot of the Austrian Alps, its UNESCO-listed old town is among the best-preserved baroque centres north of the mountains -- and provided the lakes, gardens and squares of a beloved 1965 musical about a singing family.
In a third-floor flat on a narrow guild-sign-lined shopping street here, a powdered-wig prodigy was born in 1756; his birth-house is now the city's most visited museum.
puzzles.funFact: The city's very name means 'salt fortress' -- the salt dug from the surrounding mountains was so valuable that it bankrolled the marble churches and palaces of the entire baroque old town, which is why a small Alpine town ended up looking like a miniature Rome.
puzzles.teaser: On the night the horned ones rattle their chains through the alleys, a hilltop fortress keeps watch over a town that turned a mineral into marble.

puzzles.imageDescription: A snow-blanketed cluster of timber cabins glowing with warm lights under a deep blue Arctic dusk, a painted white line curving across the frozen square to mark the Arctic Circle, with reindeer and a souvenir-laden post office nearby.
clues: A post office here fields roughly half a million letters a year from around 200 countries, and during the holiday rush it can take in some 30,000 in a single day.

In 1950 a visiting American First Lady prompted local officials to throw up a cabin on just two weeks' notice so she could experience life on the Arctic Circle, the seed from which this whole place would later grow.
The hosting town was razed almost entirely in 1944 as retreating troops left it in flames, then famously rebuilt to a plan shaped like a reindeer's head, with roads forming the antlers.
It sits about eight kilometres north of a Lapland city, and a painted line across its square lets you straddle the Arctic Circle and collect a certificate for the crossing.

Officially branded a certain jolly figure's 'hometown' only in 1985, it hands you a postmark you can get nowhere else on Earth, while reindeer wait outside and the night sky may flicker green overhead.
answers: Santa Claus House, North Pole, Alaska
puzzles.funFact: The Finnish architect Alvar Aalto rebuilt the destroyed host city after WWII using a town plan shaped like a reindeer's head, with the road network forming the antlers and the sports stadium sitting where the eye would be.
puzzles.teaser: Cross a painted line at the top of the world, where every child's letter finds an answer.
